### Claude (2026-11-10 08:30)

This is the **retail install DVD for Trainz Simulator 2010** (the "TS2010" train simulator by **Auran**), in a **Just Flight** edition. It's a Windows-only installer disc from April 2010. I only read it: nothing was run, patched or changed, and its size and date are the same as before.

One thing first: **REA can't open ISO files** (it said "unsupported binary format"). So I listed the disc's contents with 7-Zip, copied the six small program files into a temp folder, and pointed REA at those. I deleted the temp copies afterwards.

## What it is
| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| A DVD image | Standard data-disc signature (ISO 9660), disc name `TRS2010EE`, 5.76 GB (too big for a CD) |
| Trainz Simulator 2010 | `start.inf` title line: "Trainz Simulator 2010"; button "Install Trainz Simulator 2010" → `data\setup.exe` |
| Made by Auran | Installer settings: publisher "Auran", folder `Auran\TS2010`, links to `www.TS2010.com/support.html` and `/updates.html`, main program `{app}\Trainz.exe` |
| Just Flight edition | `start.exe` version info: "Just Flight, Product CD front end program 4.00.10"; link to justflight.com |
| Disc burned 19 Apr 2010 | Disc header: "NERO BURNING ROM", created 2010-04-19. The installer files are dated 16 Mar 2010 |

"EE" is probably "Engineers Edition", but that's only a guess: the disc doesn't spell it out anywhere I looked.

## What it was built with
- **Installer: Inno Setup 5.1.x.** `setup.exe` contains "Inno Setup Setup Data (5.1.10)", "InnoSetupLdrWindow" and a "JR.Inno.Setup" manifest. Its settings were compressed with LZMA. It also has a custom install script (Pascal Script) with steps like `LocateExistingInstallationPath` and `ExecTrainzUtil`.
- **Data files: Inno Setup disk slices.** All four `.bin` files start with Inno's slice marker `idska32`.
- **Menu program: Delphi.** `start.exe` is UPX-packed and has a `TForm1` window, which is a Delphi pattern.
- **Preview program: Borland C++ Builder.** `preview.exe` contains "Borland C++ – Copyright 1999 Inprise" and Delphi/VCL form classes.
- **Image libraries:** MW Graphics DLLs by Martin Wright (2003–2005), both UPX-packed.
- **`DrvMgt.dll`: Microsoft Visual C++.** It contains the Visual C++ runtime strings.

## Main parts
1. **Autorun menu.** `AUTORUN.INF` opens `start.exe`, which reads `start.inf` and shows `box.jpg` and `logo.bmp`. Only one button is switched on (Install). The others are leftovers from other Just Flight products and are hidden with `**`: FSX Airbus, VLJ Business Jet, SR-71.
2. **`Data/setup.exe` (418 KB).** This is the real installer.
3. **`Data/setup-1a.bin`, `-1b`, `-2a`, `-2b` (about 5.75 GB together).** These hold the actual game data. The "1"/"2" naming suggests it was split for two discs and later put onto one DVD (my reading of the names). Inno compressed the data, so I couldn't list the files inside without a dedicated unpacker.
4. **`preview.exe`.** The "Additional products on this DVD" viewer, turned off in `start.inf`.
5. **`DrvMgt.dll`.** Its exports are `Setup` and `Remove`, and it refers to `SECDRV.SYS`, the SafeDisc copy-protection driver. That makes it the SafeDisc driver helper. I didn't check what on the disc actually uses it.
6. **`mwgfx.dll` and `mwgfx24.dll`.** Image libraries used by the menu programs.

Nothing to commit: this chat has no repo, and I didn't save any report files.

FOLLOW-UPS: List the game files inside the setup .bin files | Look closer at the SafeDisc DrvMgt.dll | Save this as a report file

### Claude (2026-11-10 08:33)

A real native Linux version of Trainz 2010 isn't something I can make, so I haven't built anything yet. Here's why, and what I can do.

**Why a true native port won't work**
- Trainz 2010 is closed-source. The disc only has the finished Windows program (`Trainz.exe`, packed inside the installer). There's no source code to rebuild for Linux.
- The only way would be to rebuild the whole game engine from scratch so it can load the original files. That's years of work, and it would be a copy of someone else's game, which I won't build. Auran/N3V never made a Linux version either; they said there weren't enough buyers ([Auran forum](https://forums.auran.com/threads/linux-using-wine-or-steam.150807/)).

**What I can build: a game that installs and launches like a native one on Hearth OS**
You click "Trainz 2010" in your app menu and it starts. You never see Wine underneath. It would work like this:
1. **Install from your ISO.** A script reads the disc without changing it. It runs `Data\setup.exe` directly and skips the Just Flight menu (`start.exe`), because that menu brings the SafeDisc driver along, and Wine can't run that driver.
2. **Its own sealed Windows layer.** Trainz gets its own Wine setup (Wine's "prefix" folder) in your home folder, kept apart from everything else. It would use the Steam that's already installed (with Proton) or Bottles from Flatpak. Your PC runs Hearth OS as a read-only system image (I checked: `/run/ostree-booted` exists), so nothing gets installed into the system itself. That keeps booting and your settings untouched.
3. **A proper menu entry** with the game's icon, plus an uninstall script.

What people report: one user had TS2010 "running, no major issues" under an old Wine on Ubuntu ([Auran forum](https://forums.auran.com/threads/linux-using-wine-or-steam.150807/)). CodeWeavers lists it as "manual install required" with an out-of-date rating ([CodeWeavers](https://codeweavers.com/compatibility/crossover/trainz-2010)). There's also a TrainzOnline guide for Debian that gives each Trainz install its own Wine setup ([TrainzOnline wiki](https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/HowTo/Installing_Trainz_at_Linux:_Debian_based_Distributions)). That's encouraging, but nothing recent confirms it works.

Some things are still unknown:
- **Your graphics chip.** It's an Intel Alder Lake-N (UHD Graphics). It should handle a 2010 DirectX 9 game, but I can't promise smooth speed.
- **Serial key and activation.** I don't know yet whether TS2010 still needs online activation, or whether those servers still work.

While I wait for your answer, I'm handing out the research:

@Gemini Look up Trainz Simulator 2010 (TS2010) running under Wine or Proton: the DLLs or winetricks it needs (d3dx9, vcrun, .NET?), known crashes, and the settings that work best on Intel graphics. Give your sources.
@Grok Find out whether TS2010 (Auran, 2010, Just Flight disc edition) needs a serial number or online activation, whether those servers still work in 2026, and whether the game itself (not the disc menu) uses SafeDisc. Give your sources.
@ChatGPT When I write the installer and launcher scripts, review them. For now, check this plan for gaps.

**Your call:** should I go ahead with the "installs and launches like a native game" version? And should it use Steam/Proton (already installed) or Bottles (one Flatpak to add)? I'd pick Steam/Proton, since nothing new has to be installed.

If you'd like a truly native train game, I can build an original train simulator for Linux with my own engine and content instead. It just wouldn't be Trainz.

FOLLOW-UPS: Yes, build it with Steam/Proton | Use Bottles instead | Tell me more about an original Linux train sim

### Claude (2026-11-10 08:36)

The installer on the disc lists every file it puts on your PC: 886 files in the game folder. The file names alone show the engine's main parts. I unpacked only that list, not the game files, so I haven't looked inside `Trainz.exe` or any DLL yet. Everything below comes from file names. The ISO is unchanged and I deleted my temp files.

## The engine, part by part

**Main programs and files**
- `Trainz.exe` is the game itself; there's a copy in the main folder and in `bin\`.
- `bin\TrainzUtil.exe` is a command-line helper that the installer runs 11 times during setup.
- `bin\TADDaemon.exe` is very likely the background program for the Trainz Asset Database, the catalogue of all trains and scenery. The asset index itself is `UserData\assets.tdx`.
- `TrainzDiag.exe` (diagnostics) and `XCrashReport.exe` (crash reporter).
- Settings live in `Trainz.cfg` and `trainzoptions.txt`.
- The game's content is packed into `.ja` archives: `Base.ja`, `Data.ja` and `Builtin\1.ja` to `8.ja`.

**Graphics**
- The drawing code is split into layers: `RenderSystem`, `Render2DCore`, `Render3DCore`, `Render3DFoundation` and `Render3DExtension` (all ending in `_7c.dll`).
- It has two graphics back ends: `RenderDirectX9_7c.dll` and **`RenderOpenGL_7c.dll`**.
- `plugins\TNISpeedTree.dll` draws trees, with 17 shader files (`.fx`) in `SpeedTreeShaders\`.
- `WaterSystem_7c.dll` (water), `nvtt.dll` (NVIDIA's texture tools), `VFWMoviePlayer_7c.dll` (video playback).
- The installer also runs Microsoft's DirectX setup: 137 `.cab` packages, such as `d3dx9_25` and `d3dx9_30`.

**Sound**
- `SoundCore_7c.dll`, plus two DirectSound back ends: `SoundDS8_7c.dll` and `SoundDS3D_7c.dll`.
- I found no OpenAL or FMOD files, so sound goes only through Microsoft DirectSound.

**Input**
- **No separate input file exists.** There's no DirectInput, joystick or RailDriver DLL in the list.
- Keyboard and mouse handling must therefore be inside `Trainz.exe`. I'd have to unpack that file to confirm it.

**Networking**
- `libeay32.dll` and `ssleay32.dll` are OpenSSL, used for secure web connections.
- `bin\mozilla\` holds a full built-in Firefox-style browser engine (161 files, including `xul.dll`, `nss3.dll`, `js3250.dll` and `necko_http.xpt`). The game uses it for its built-in web pages and online store.
- The installer's terms text names the **Auran Download Station**, the online content service run by N3V Games. It also links to `ts2009.com` and `TS2010.com` for updates.
- I found nothing that points to multiplayer.

**Scripts**
- `scripts\` holds 97 `.gs` files in Trainz's own script language, for example `asset.gs`, `Bogey.gs`, `Cabin.gs`, `BaseIndustry.gs`, `browser.gs`.
- `libraries\` holds 97 `.gsl` files, probably the compiled versions of those scripts (the counts match).
- `Lexer_7c.dll` is probably part of the script compiler.
- `trainznativeinterface.dll` probably links the scripts to the engine.
- `CMPData\tools\*.bat` belong to the content tools (Content Manager).

**Built with**
- Microsoft Visual C++ 2005 (`msvcr80`, `msvcp80` and MFC 8.0) and some Visual C++ 2003 (`msvcr71`).
- `MSCOMCTL.OCX` and `COMDLG32.OCX` are old Visual Basic 6 controls, probably for the launcher or tools.

## What this means for running it on Linux
The **built-in OpenGL back end** matters most. If the game can be set to OpenGL in `trainzoptions.txt`, it would skip DirectX 9 entirely, which usually runs better and is easier under Wine/Proton. The weak spot is the built-in browser, which tends to be the hardest part to get working under Wine. I haven't tested any of this.

Gemini stopped before answering my earlier research request. The next step is unpacking `Trainz.exe` (read-only, into a temp folder) and checking it with REA, to settle the input question and find the setting that switches to OpenGL.

FOLLOW-UPS: Unpack Trainz.exe and check its imports | Find the OpenGL switch in trainzoptions.txt | Go ahead with the Steam/Proton launcher

I've written the engine map to `docs/ENGINE-MAP.md` and pushed it to this chat's branch `hearth/use-the-rea-tools-to-look-at-4c82`. The ISO was only read (it's unchanged and is detached again).

**How it was done:** REA read the program files' import, export and resource tables. REA's decompiler couldn't run, because it accepts Ghidra 12.1.x and this PC has 12.2. So the code addresses come from `objdump` disassembly plus small read-only Python scripts. `bin\trainz.exe` has no function names, so its addresses are the places that use a string, not named functions.

**There are no `.big` files.** The archives are **`.ja`** files: `Base.ja`, `Data.ja` and `Builtin\1.ja` to `8.ja`.

1. **Content and lookup.** You're right that every asset has a KUID and a config file, with three additions:
   - There are two KUID forms: `<kuid:user:content>` and `<kuid2:user:content:version>`.
   - Built-in assets mostly carry `config.chump`, a binary version of `config.txt`.
   - Inside the archives each asset sits in a `hash-XX/kuid …` folder, where XX is the 8 bytes of the KUID XOR-ed together. That matched all 499 folders I tested.
   - The asset index is `UserData\assets.tdx`, kept by the `TADDaemon.exe` database service.
2. **File formats.**
   - **`.ja` is fully worked out:** a header, one block per file and an index at the end. Packed files use Byte Pair Encoding, a small 1994 compression scheme; the unpacker is at `0x1000d130` in `KernelStandard_7c.dll`.
   - **3D models (`.im`, `.pm`), textures (`.texture`) and animations (`.kin`)** share one chunked container, and I mapped its top-level layout.
   - **Routes (`mapfile.gnd/.obs/.trk/.bmk`), sessions (`profile.*`), sounds (`.wav`, `.mp3`) and scripts (`.gs`, `.gsl`, `.gse`):** headers and the code that loads them are identified.
3. **Systems.**
   - **Graphics:** DirectX 9 (`d3dx9_42`) and an **OpenGL** back end (using NVIDIA's Cg shader library).
   - **Sound:** DirectSound 8 and DirectSound 3D.
   - **Input:** DirectInput 8 and plain Win32.
   - **Scripting:** Trainz's own script language. The compiler and the engine that runs scripts seem to be inside `trainz.exe`.
   - **Networking:** basic Windows sockets, OpenSSL and a built-in Firefox-style browser engine.
   - **Content tools:** the database service plus Content Manager.
4. **Exe and DLLs.** `bin\trainz.exe` (6.5 MB) is the game itself. The engine, Auran's own "Jet" engine, is split into about 25 `_7c.dll` files, loaded as plugins listed in `plugins.ini`. The 64 KB `Trainz.exe` in the main folder is only a launcher.

The document ends with a 14-step porting order. It starts with the `.ja` reader and the config readers, then textures, models and routes. The script language, the in-game UI and networking come last.

**Corrections to my earlier answers:**
- There **are** separate input DLLs; my first text scan missed them.
- The checksum in each `.ja` file entry is **not CRC32**, and I don't know what it is yet.

**Not verified yet:**
- I proved the `.ja` decoder on two files decoding to their exact sizes, plus about 30 samples of every file type that came out with valid headers. The full pass over every file never finished.
- I didn't decode the insides of models, terrain, sessions or compiled scripts. The document lists all the open questions.
- No GitHub Actions run is expected, since this push only adds a document.

**Next steps:**
- My unpacked copies (783 MB) are still in `/tmp/trs_work_x3bS` for follow-ups. I can delete them whenever you like.
- For function names inside `trainz.exe`, install Ghidra 12.1.x so REA's decompiler works.
- I'm happy to keep building readers and converters for these formats. Rebuilding the Trainz engine itself is still the part I won't write, as I said earlier.

I've built the read-only `.ja` archive reader with a command-line tool, tests and a CI workflow. All four CI jobs pass on Debian 13: gcc and clang, each in a normal build and an AddressSanitizer + UBSan build. The code is on this chat's branch `hearth/use-the-rea-tools-to-look-at-4c82`, with pull request [#1](https://github.com/Dragongamer9/TS2010/pull/1) open against `main` and not merged.

You asked for a new branch, but this chat may only push to its own `hearth/` branch, so I used that. The pull request already existed; the app opened it under the chat's name, "Use the REA tools to look at…", so you may want to rename it. I couldn't compile on this PC, so CI was the first real build. The first run failed to link the clang sanitizer build because a Debian package was missing; I added `libclang-rt-dev` and the next run passed.

**What's in it**
- **`src/content/JaArchive.{h,cpp}`**: opens an archive, lists it, finds a file by name or KUID, and reads a file whole or streams it. Bad files give a clear error, never a crash, and nothing is read past the end of a file. The archive's index is read with a single seek and kept in memory, so the hard drive doesn't jump around.
- **Matches the game:** I traced these in `KernelStandard_7c.dll`; the addresses are in `docs/formats/ja.md`.
  - Names are lowercased (`A`–`Z` only), `\` and `/` are both accepted, and `.` and `..` are resolved.
  - If two files have the same name, the first one in the index wins.
  - Compression is detected by the data starting with `CFIL`, not by the flag. Older version-0x101 archives have a shorter header, and the decoder handles that.
- **`tools/ja_tool.cpp`**: commands `info`, `list`, `find`, `kuid`, `cat`, `verify` and `extract`.
  - `extract` writes only under `~/.local/share/trainz-native/`. It refuses any folder inside the Trainz install or `TRAINZ_DATA_DIR`, and never overwrites a file.
  - Game files are only ever opened read-only.
- **Tests**: 40 run in CI on small archives the tests build themselves, with no game files in the repo.
  - One test cuts the archive short at every possible length and changes every byte, and checks that it never crashes.
  - Four tests against the real install skip themselves unless `TRAINZ_DATA_DIR` is set.
- **The format document and the engine map**: `docs/formats/ja.md` notes what each part is based on. I also applied ChatGPT's six corrections to `docs/ENGINE-MAP.md`, including the missing train-simulation stage.

**What I couldn't confirm**
- **The C++ reader has never run on real game files.** CI only uses the made-up archives. The Python prototype is what was checked on the real `Base.ja`, `Data.ja` and `Builtin/8.ja`. Please run this once on your dad's PC (it only reads):
  ```sh
  TRAINZ_DATA_DIR=/path/to/TS2010 ctest --test-dir build -R RealInstall --output-on-failure
  ```
- **Every file decoding correctly isn't proven yet.** No full pass has finished. `TRAINZ_FULL_VERIFY=1` does one; it's about 7 GB, so it's slow on a hard drive.
- **Some rules come only from reading the code.** The three archives have no duplicate names, backslashes or leading `/`, so "first one wins" has never been seen in real data. Version-0x101 archives also weren't available to test.
- **Still unknown:** what the per-file checksum is, what the `FIL!` tag means, and what the last header field means.
- **The KUID folder rule (`hash-XX`) is only observed.** It matched all 499 folders I tested, but I haven't traced the code that builds it; the real-install test checks it on every folder. Which version of an asset wins when there are several is also unknown.
- **Two small edge cases:** I didn't fully trace the drive-letter case (`X:`) in the name cleanup, which doesn't occur in archives. For a name that isn't terminated, the game stops loading the index; my reader stops with an error instead.

My unpacked copies of the disc files (about 783 MB) are still in `/tmp/trs_work_x3bS`. Nothing has been merged; that's yours to do.

**What's new**
- **`src/content/AssetConfig`** reads both formats into one tree of named values: text, numbers, KUIDs, raw bytes and groups.
  - **The `.chump` rules come from the game's own code** (`trainz.exe` `0x7ff710` and `0x7ff1f0`). It checks the `ACS$` header, then reads items as size, key, type byte and value.
  - **Value types and KUID packing come from the data.** The version sits in the top 7 bits of the user number, and version 0 means a plain KUID. KUIDs stored as text, such as `<KUID2:33404:22112:02>` or a bare `37028:27013`, are also accepted.
  - Damaged files give a clear error, never a crash. The tests cut files short at every length and change every byte.
- **`config-tool show`** prints any config, loose or inside a `.ja` archive. **`config-tool kuid`** prints the asset's own KUID. Both only read.
- **A new real-install test** parses every config in the install and checks that each asset's KUID matches its folder.
- **`docs/formats/config.md`** describes the format and what each rule is based on.

**`model-viewer`**
- **What it does:** it opens a model straight from a `.ja` archive and puts its textures on it. Drag with the mouse to turn it, scroll to zoom, press **W** for wireframe and **Esc** or **Q** to quit. With `--kin` it plays the animation, and **space** pauses it.
- **What it uses:** SDL2 and plain OpenGL 2.1, both from Debian packages. That should run on your dad's Radeon R9 390 with Debian's standard drivers.
- **It only reads:** it doesn't write any files.

**It needs a first try on a real screen**, and I can't do that from here. On Hearth OS the build has to happen inside a Debian 13 toolbox, since the system itself can't take `apt install`:

```sh
toolbox create -d debian -r 13 trainz && toolbox enter trainz
sudo apt install cmake ninja-build g++ libgtest-dev libsdl2-dev libgl-dev git
git clone https://github.com/Dragongamer9/TS2010.git && cd TS2010
git checkout hearth/use-the-rea-tools-to-look-at-4c82
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build
./build/model-viewer testdata/ts2010/Builtin/sample8.ja "hash-c1/kuid 58422 50128/benthd.pm" --kin "hash-c1/kuid 58422 50128/anim.kin"
```

That last command should show the bogie with its wheels turning. Tell me what you see, especially if textures look upside down or the model appears sideways; both are easy to fix. You need your GitHub login for `git clone`, since the repo is private. The `toolbox create` line may differ slightly depending on what Hearth OS ships; if it fails, paste the error and I'll adjust.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **REA MCP tools:**
     - can't open ISOs;
     - can't decompile: Ghidra 12.2 is installed, but REA needs 12.1.x;
     - used for PE import, export and resource tables;
     - `objdump` disassembly used instead.
   - **Installer and engine:**
     - Inno Setup 5.1.x; `innoextract` from Debian `.deb` files (extracted into a temp folder, plus a boost library);
     - the ISO is mounted read-only via `udisksctl`;
     - Auran's "Jet" engine (`*_7c.dll` plugins via `plugins.ini`, `JetGetPlugins`);
     - DirectX 9 and OpenGL (Cg) back ends; DirectSound; DirectInput 8;
     - TrainzScript (`.gs`/`.gsl`/`.gse`), TNI, OpenSSL, Gecko.
   - **`.ja` archive:**
     - "ARCH" "INFO" (32 bytes, ARC0, version 0x101–0x102, file count, index offset, a field 42203/42195 of unknown meaning);
     - "FIL " blocks: name[260], original size, stored size, hash (unknown; not CRC32), 12 reserved bytes, flags (0x80 = compressed);
     - "IDX " index: 296-byte rows, lowercase names;
     - lookups: `_strlwr`, canonicalize `\`/`/`/`.`/`..`, name hash `h = (h << 3) ^ signed char`, first duplicate wins.
   - **CFIL compression:** "CFIL", version, original size; 16 KiB blocks, each with a u16 header (0x8000 = raw); the packed blocks use Byte Pair Encoding (Gage's variant: a skip doesn't also read a pair; 256-entry stack).
   - **KUIDs:**
     - folder `hash-XX` = XOR of the KUID's 8 bytes (observed only);
     - plain vs kuid2: plain iff (version 0 and user ≥ 0) or (version 127 and user < 0) (traced, `TADDaemon.exe` 0x51919a);
     - chump packing: user = signed 25-bit, version = top 7 bits;
     - loose text forms accepted.
   - **`.chump`:** "ACS$", u32 version, u32 reserved, u32 body size; items = u32 size, u8 key length, key, u8 type, value. Types: 0 group, 1 ints, 2 floats, 3 string (padded with NULs), 4 binary, 5 null, 13 kuid. The item walk was traced at `trainz.exe` 0x7ff1f0.
   - **`config.txt` grammar:** observed only. Strings may span lines, and a string may start on the next line.
   - **JIRF container:** "JIRF" u32 size, form, then chunks with no padding. A trailer after the declared size is ignored.
   - **`.texture` (MMTF):**
     - INFO words: 0 version (0x103/0x106/0x107), 2 mip count, 4 format, 5 width, 6 height;
     - MMAP mips stored smallest first;
     - format ids from the Jet name list: 1 ARGB8888, 3 RGB0888, 10/11/12 DXT1/3/5, others by name only.
   - **Mesh (IDXM):**
     - INFO; CHNK (u32 100, index) holding MATL and GEOM; NINF in `.pm`;
     - GEOM v101 (header 7 words), v102 (8), v200 (9 + name block), v201 (10, flags; flag 1 adds an extra 12-byte array per vertex at the end);
     - then vertices (x, y, z, u, v; 20 bytes), u16 indices, vertex normals, face normals;
     - MATL v102/103: name, 16 floats, textures (type, path, amount); text length bit 30 = UTF-16;
     - Z is up.
   - **`.kin` (ANIM):**
     - INFO: version 100, source name, frames, fps, a float;
     - EVNT: frame, flags, name;
     - SKEL: nested BONE tree;
     - FRAM: position + quaternion per bone;
     - bone positions taken as absolute: not confirmed.
   - **`mapfile.gnd`:**
     - "GND\r", section count, two signed words that vary per route;
     - 20-byte index entries (reversed tag Sec5/Secs, start, end, x, y);
     - per section: data, then an 8,192-byte 64×64 u16 overview map (BGR565 observed);
     - section loaders at `trainz.exe` 0x81ec70 / 0x8298c0 (not traced).
   - **Damaged files:**

I added a reader for the game's key bindings (`keyboard.txt`) and pushed it to PR #1. CI passed on commit `3cdd32c`: 156 of 156 tests on all four builds (gcc and clang, release and ASan/UBSan), none skipped.

**What's new**
- **The reader** (`src/input/KeyBindings.{h,cpp}`) reads Dad's `UserData/settings/keyboard.txt`. It knows every key name in the game's own name list inside `trainz.exe` (near file offset 0x543b10), so spellings like `pgup`, `KPPgUp`, `fullstop` and `kpdn` all work, in any case.
- **On the real file** it reads all 6 groups and 383 actions, and every key name is recognised. `RealInstall.KeyboardBindingsRead` checks this in CI on an unchanged copy of the file, now in `testdata/` (the repo is private).

- **Tests and docs:** new tests (`tests/test_keybindings.cpp`) cover the key names, combos, unbound keys, the odd line, and damaged input that must not crash it. The format is written up in `docs/formats/keyboard.md`.
- **ChatGPT's last review is applied:** `sound-player` now builds whenever SDL2 is installed, and the roadmap now reads "5,870 of 5,874 WAVs decode, 4 refused". That edit had an extra `endif()` in `CMakeLists.txt`, which would have broken the build; I removed it before pushing.

  - Shift, Ctrl and Alt must match exactly, so Shift+W doesn't fire an action bound to W.
  - Left and right Shift, Ctrl and Alt count the same.
  - These matching rules are my choice; I haven't traced the game's own rules.
- **SDL mapping:** `src/input/SdlKeys` ties each key name to a physical key. The game reads keys by physical position too (it uses DirectInput 8), so a binding stays on the same key whatever the keyboard layout. A test checks that every key name maps to its own key and back.
- **Two new tools:**
  - `input-tool list / shared / press` shows the bindings, lists keys bound to more than one action, and answers what a press does. For example, `input-tool press keyboard.txt driver "alt 1"` gives `train_cabin_aws_isolate`.
  - `key-tester keyboard.txt` opens a small window and prints the actions for each key you press.
- **Bug caught by the new tests:** the reader didn't accept its own key names (like `LeftShift`) when reading them back. Fixed.

**Found in Dad's file:** 52 key combinations are bound to more than one action in the same group: 15 in driver, 27 in surveyor, 5 in menu and 5 in standard_dialog. **What the game's code shows**
- **How a line is read:** each character is lowercased with `tolower`. A comma ends a combo and a space ends a word; nothing else separates words, so a tab becomes part of a word. Each word is then applied in order to the combo:
  - `ctrl`, `control`, `alt` and `shift` add a modifier;
  - a key name sets the key, replacing any earlier one;
  - `null` or an unknown word clears the whole combo, modifiers included.
- **`camera_car  alt ctrl shift c a r z` is ctrl+alt+shift+Z.** `c`, `a` and `r` are ordinary key names, and each one replaces the one before, so Z wins. That is what the reader already did, but now it's traced, not a guess.
- **Exactly 141 key names are accepted**, covering 98 keys. My reader had also accepted 27 the game never does, such as `page up`, `kp/`, `.`, `~` and `f13`–`f15`. Those are gone, so the reader now matches the game exactly. The full list is in `docs/formats/keyboard.md`.
- **The game numbers keys by position.** For 80 of the 98 keys, its code is the DirectInput key number plus one; the other 18 keep the same order. So it most likely binds physical keys, as the port does. What I couldn't find is where it converts a live key press into its own number, so behaviour on a non-US keyboard still isn't proven.

<result>I've traced and decoded the route section data, and every section on the disc fits the layout exactly. It's committed as `ceed2a4` on branch `worktree-agent-a5cdf97c31369499c`, not pushed, with no AI attribution lines.

**Fraction explained:** 100% of the section bytes are now accounted for by fields read from the disassembly. The meaning of a few fields is still a guess (listed below).

**Sections validated:**
- All 15,243 sections in the 50 `mapfile.gnd` files from `Builtin\1.ja`–`8.ja` (653,817,764 bytes) end exactly at their end offset. Both the Python checker and the C++ reader give the same result.
- 623 more sections in two older `.gnd` files (versions 10 and 11) also fit, but only in the Python checker. The C++ reader refuses versions below 12 because their overview map size isn't worked out.

**The old reading had the index grouped wrongly.** Byte 3 of the file is a version number (13 on every route). Each index entry is `{x, y, tag, start, end}`, not `{tag, start, end, x, y}`. So the "two signed header words" were just section 0's position. The "duplicate positions" (one in the sample, five routes across the disc) didn't really exist. The start and end offsets were right before. The game never checks the "GND" bytes. The 0x81ec70 and 0x8298c0 you named only create the objects; the actual readers are 0x82be00 (Secs) and 0x821200 (Sec5), and sections are loaded on demand from the stored start offset.

**Section data fields:**

| Field | Evidence |
|---|---|
| `u32 slotCount` (always 250), then up to 250 × `{f32 weight; if weight &gt; 0: u32 content, u32 packed user/version}` | read in the disassembly, checked on every section. The KUID word order is the reverse of `.chump`; reader at 0x80c8d0 |
| `u32 cellCount` (more than 1,296 counts as 0), then × `{u16 col, u16 row, f32 value}`; cells outside 0..35 are ignored | read in the disassembly, checked; what the value means is a guess (perhaps water level) |
| 76×76 (Secs) or 148×148 (Sec5) vertices | count read in the disassembly, checked; row-by-row grid seen in the data (neighbour heights smooth at stride 1 and at row length) |
| Vertex: `0xFE` = texture, extra, height 0; `0xFD` = texture, extra, f32 height; otherwise a list of `{weight, extra, next texture}` ending at 0xFF, then f32 height (game keeps the first 3 layers, stops after 33) | read in the disassembly (0x6f0e50, and the writer 0x6f0cb0 agrees), checked |
| Overview map: 64×64 u16, the game expands bits 11-15 / 5-10 / 0-4 into three colour bytes (0x6e4070) | read in the disassembly; which byte is red is still only seen in data |
| "Height in metres", "blend weight", the 10 m / 5 m grid spacing and border | guesses, labelled as such in route.md |

**Changes:**
- `docs/formats/route.md` rewritten with addresses for every field, the correction explained, and the evidence class marked on each field.
- `tools/dev/gnd_sections.py` added as the checker. It reads `.gnd` files, folders or `.ja` archives without changing them.
- `src/content/GroundFile` now reads the index the traced way, keeps the version, and has a new `parseGroundSection` that errors if parsing doesn't end exactly at the section end.
- `tests/test_ground.cpp` is rewritten (8 tests, which pass under g++ with AddressSanitizer). The real-install test now decodes every section too, but I only syntax-checked it, since there's no cmake to build the full suite.

### Claude (2026-11-11 00:02)

I added a reader for `.texture.txt` texture descriptors, and it handles every descriptor on the disc. CI passed on `2dd47d2` on all four builds: 228 of 228 tests. In each build all 360 descriptors were combined with no problems. ChatGPT asked for no changes on the last round.

**What these files are:** small text files that name the image a texture uses (`Primary`) and, optionally, where its transparency comes from (`Alpha`). They also carry hints such as how it tiles and how it's filtered.

**Read from the game's code (`RenderSystem_7c.dll`)**
- **Keys:** the game knows 16 keys. I took their value words and the number the engine stores for each one straight from the game's tables, for example `AlphaHint`: opaque = 0, semitransparent = 1, masked = 2. Values are compared without regard to case, and an unknown word leaves the setting unchanged.
- **`Tile`:** if the key is present, the texture first stops repeating in both directions. Then an `s` anywhere in the value makes it repeat sideways, and a `t` makes it repeat up-and-down. So `st` repeats both ways and `none` repeats neither.

**Taken from the official wiki, not from the code**
- How the colour image and the transparency image combine:
  - `Primary` alone is fully opaque;
  - `Alpha` naming the same file uses that file's own transparency;
  - a different `Alpha` file is used as a grey transparency mask, and the sizes must match.
- This matches the 165 TGAs whose alpha is empty: used without `Alpha`, they show opaque.

**Checked on the disc:** there are 360 descriptors, all in `Base.ja`; the `Builtin` archives use compiled `.texture` files instead. Every descriptor's images are found next to it, decode, and combine. `texture-tool info` and `png` now accept descriptors. I exported a crate texture with a separate transparency mask, and it looks right: slats with see-through gaps.

**Roadmap:** step 4 (textures) goes from 75% to 85%. Overall is 27.85 ÷ 102 = 27.30%, so it stays at **27%**.

**Not confirmed yet**
- The exact line format the game accepts. Every disc file uses `Key=value`, but the general-purpose text parser the game reads them with isn't traced.
- The game's own code for combining the colour and transparency images.
- The default value when a key is missing.

online.ts2009

Start with one simple scenery class.

wikibooks

Separate track geometry from connectivity.
For .trk, use a straight stretch, a moved endpoint, two connected stretches, two disconnected stretches, and a junction. Your reported stretch/vertex container split gives a useful starting point, but endpoint-reference encoding still needs tracing or controlled evidence.

Keep TrainzMap as a secondary lead.

I labelled the "adds up as you turn it" idea as a hypothesis, and found which way object rotation turns. Both are pushed. CI passed on `baf2814`: 243 of 243 tests on all four builds. Progress stays at **29%**.

**ChatGPT's point (`a863daa`):** the format doc and code comments now call the "keeps adding up as an object is turned" explanation a **hypothesis only**. Values beyond one full turn are a fact; why they happen isn't known.

**Which way objects turn (`baf2814`)**
- **The test:** buildings next to track are usually lined up with it. I paired 11,376 buildings with the nearest track piece, using only track that runs at an angle (track running north–south or east–west can't tell the two directions apart). Then I compared each building's rotation with the track's direction.
- **The result:** read as turning anticlockwise, the rotation lines up with the track for 23.6% of buildings in a single 2° band. Read as turning clockwise, it's almost flat (3.2%, where 2.2% is chance). So **positive rotation turns anticlockwise**, the same way as angles in maths.
- **Still unknown:**
  - which side of a model faces east at rotation 0. Line-ups only tell me the model is square to the world's axes, not which side is its front;
  - why the values go past one full turn (still a hypothesis).

**Older trains (from older sessions)**
- **Why it needed a different approach:** the older format doesn't store how long each vehicle record is, so the reader can't simply step from one vehicle to the next. Instead it **finds vehicles by a fixed pattern** that comes after each vehicle's ID. It accepts a train only if:
  - the number of vehicles found equals the count the train says it has;
  - the first vehicle starts where it should;
  - every vehicle has a valid name.
- **Result:** **606 of 826** old trains decode (2,977 vehicles); the other **220 are refused** rather than guessed. This is a heuristic, and the docs say so plainly.
- **Checked on one old session:** "Frühdienst Teil 2" on the route "Winter in Deutschland". All 12 trains name a track piece that exists on the route, and each first vehicle stands within 0.1 m of that piece's line. That's one session per format, so it's evidence, not proof.

### Claude (2026-11-11 06:41)

Checking why `asset-tool find` printed nothing turned up a real bug: **500 assets were missing from the asset index**. It's fixed, the 3D view now draws more than three times as many models, and progress reaches **33%**. Pushed, and CI passed on `256a17e`: 261 of 261 tests on all four builds.

**ChatGPT's wording point:** "all of a model's parts" was my chat summary. The docs already said "full-detail daytime" parts; the one code comment that read broadly now says "eligible full-detail daytime parts".

**The missing assets**
- **What was wrong:** most configs write their own KUID as `<kuid:…>`, but 488 on the disc write it as a bare number (`kuid 101135`), or a number in quotes. The reader rejected those, so the whole asset was left out of the index.
- **Evidence for the fix:** in every one of the 488 whose folder is named after a KUID, the folder is `kuid _1 <that number>`. So a bare number means `<kuid:-1:number>`, where −1 is N3V's built-in user. This is observed from folder names, not traced in the game.
- **Result:**
  - **no asset is dropped any more**, down from 500;
  - the index holds **19,282 assets**, up from 18,264, and **every KUID matches its folder name**.

  New tests cover both forms.
- **The `asset-tool` part:** `find` used to print nothing when no asset matched. It now says so, and points to `asset-tool versions` when other versions exist.

**Effect on the 3D view:** on the test route, **856 objects are now drawn as real models**, up from 246, with only 13 left as dots. Most of the missing ones were trees and houses that use bare-number KUIDs. Both 3D screenshots in `docs/screenshots/` are updated. The test route now shows rows of trees along the yard and hillsides, and a town full of houses.

**Roadmap:** step 3 (asset index) goes from 60% to 65%. Overall is 33.25 ÷ 102 = 32.60%, which rounds to **33%**.

Next, the biggest visual step left: **real textures on the models** instead of one flat colour per part. The renderer needs three additions:
- **UV coordinates per vertex.** The meshes already store them.
- **A small copy of each texture.** I'll decode one mip around 64–128 pixels, which keeps memory reasonable.
- **Perspective-correct sampling**, so textures don't swim across large triangles.

Leaves on many trees are cut out with alpha, so I'll alpha-test, but only when a texture has a real mix of clear and solid pixels. That avoids hiding the 165 TGAs whose alpha is 0 everywhere. That rule is a heuristic, and I'll label it. Starting with the renderer:

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Key bindings (`keyboard.txt`), traced in `trainz.exe`:**
     - the splitter at VA 0x4d5bb0: tolower; `,` ends a combo; space ends a word;
     - the word parser at 0x4d4b60: 141 key names → engine codes, where 80 of 98 are DIK+1; unknown words and `null` clear the combo; the last key word wins.
   - **Object container** (`trainz.exe` 0x886be0): version 1–5, an extra word if ≥5, items {i32 index (−1 ends), reversed tag, KUID (content, packed user), u32 size, payload}, and a tail if ≥4. Used by `.gnd` world, `.obs`, `.trk`, `profile.dat` and `profile.*`.
   - **Terrain grid (observed):** vertex = row × side + col; columns +x, rows +y; side − 4 cells (72/144) with shared edges (81% of edges match; 19% unexplained); 10 m spacing; 720 m baseboards.
   - **Track (observed):**
     - tkVx: v3, i16 bx/by, f32 x/y/z, then 4 links {i32 piece, u8 flag} + u8;
     - tkSt: version, from, to, KUID, rest;
     - tkBr = u32 2 + an embedded stretch.
   - **Placed objects (observed):** an 8-byte header (0 for mobs), then u8 flag, i16 bx/by, f32 x/y/z, f32 yaw. Yaw is radians, unwrapped, anticlockwise (inferred); the zero axis is known only mod 90°.
   - **Sessions (`profile.dat`, observed):**
     - layout: version, then 3/4/5 size-prefixed blocks;
     - behaviours (BHVR): name + chump;
     - trains (trCt), version 5 (magic 0xcaffa1da): track piece, distance, direction, vehicles {KUID, 0, 0, size, record (name at offset 41)};
     - old trains found by pattern, with safeguards: count match, first at byte 20, valid name, x/y inside the board, neighbour gap < 50 m; record versions 1/4/5.
   - **Bare-number KUIDs:** `kuid 101135` = `<kuid:-1:101135>`. 1,006 checked against folder names (1,005 bare, 1 quoted); 12 in Base/Data unconfirmed. The index's warnings are capped at 500, with `warningCount()` for the total.
   - **3D preview:** the software renderer SceneRender (perspective, depth buffer, sun shading). RouteScene builds the view. AssetMeshes handles mesh selection:
     - top-level `mesh`, or mesh-table entries without `lod-level` > 0, `night-mesh-base`, `att` or shadow, else `asset-filename` + `.im`;
     - `.lm` → `.lm.txt` highest level;
     - Paint Shed reskin → second KUID in `skin.dat`;
     - SpeedTree `.srt` → placeholder cone.
   - **Vehicles in the view:** heading from neighbouring vehicles; train models are long along +y, so yaw = heading − 90°; height taken from the track piece (a preview approximation).

Bogeys and mesh attachments: documentation findings

Scope: documentation relevant to the TS2010-era implementation. The Trainz Wiki is maintained across releases, so a current page is not automatically evidence of exact TS2010 behavior. Version limitations and unresolved details are noted below.

1. Bogey subcontainer names identify attachment points

Source: Trainz Wiki, “Bogeys” container

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/%22Bogeys%22_container

Quote:

“The bogeys container is a list of bogey subcontainers and is used by KIND Traincar assets. Each bogey subcontainer has a unique tag name and these tag names are matched with bogie attachments in the traincar mesh. These are a.bog0, a.bog1, etc.”
online.ts2009

Interpretation: resolve subcontainer “0” to a.bog0, “1” to a.bog1, and so on, using the subcontainer name rather than its position in the parsed list. The page’s examples use numeric names 0, 1, 2 and 3 and explicitly discuss their corresponding a.bog attachment points.
online.ts2009

The bogey tag selects the asset:

“Specifies the bogie asset to use at the attachment point.”
online.ts2009

The first two attachment points also have a special role in positioning the vehicle on track:

“a.bog0 and a.bog1 are used for the two end bogies, and will locate the vehicle on the track.”
online.ts2009

Do not generalize that statement into “the physically outermost visible bogies always use 0 and 1.” The same page’s GG1 example assigns 0 and 1 to the main power bogies and 2 and 3 to the leading and trailing unpowered bogies. Its steam-locomotive example also uses an invisible a.bog1 to obtain the desired vehicle alignment.
online.ts2009

Implementation implication: matching by numeric subcontainer name is documented, not merely a guess. Matching by enumeration order is not the documented rule.

2. reversed reverses animation; attachment orientation supplies the physical reversal

Source: Trainz Wiki, “Bogeys” container, reversed
https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/%22Bogeys%22_container#reversed

Quote:

“Reverses the animation direction. Used when the bogie attachment point in the traincar asset has been rotated 180 degrees around the Z axis. 1 is reversed. 0 is not reversed and the default value.”
online.ts2009

The page’s troubleshooting section explicitly separates rotating the attachment point from setting reversed:

“Have you by any chance rotated the attachment point by 180 degrees in your 3D editor to get the bogie to appear the other way round, but not set ‘reversed 1’ in the config container for that bogie?”
online.ts2009

It adds:

“You should also be able to spot this case because your wheels will be rotating the wrong way...”
online.ts2009

Implementation implication: do not implement reversed 1 as an unconditional additional 180-degree geometry rotation based on these sources. The documented operation is animation-direction reversal, used to compensate for an attachment point that is already rotated. This is a semantic correction to the stated assumption “reversed means turned 180°.”
online.ts2009

The related rotation-permitted flag has a different purpose:

“Allows the bogey to rotate itself in the Z axis to align with track direction. If 1 (default) then the bogey will rotate and if 0 then the bogey will not rotate.”
online.ts2009

Thus attachment orientation, animation reversal, and track-following rotation are separate concepts.

3. Omitted att-parent resolves to the mesh-table entry named default

Source: Trainz Wiki, “mesh-table” container

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/%22mesh-table%22_container

Quote:

“The att-parent defaults to ‘default’ which is the parent mesh.”
online.ts2009

The dedicated att-parent section repeats:

“Default: Defaults to ‘default’ which is the parent mesh”

“The tag tells Trainz in which mesh the attachment point is located.”
online.ts2009

The att section explains the distinction between naming a parent mesh and selecting an attachment point:

“The mesh (and animation if present) is inserted at a mesh attachment point rather than the origin (without this line the mesh is placed relative to the origin of the parent model).”
online.ts2009

Implementation implication: when att-parent is omitted, use the mesh-table entry named default as the parent. When att is omitted, placement is relative to the parent model’s origin rather than a named attachment point. These excerpts do not specify a fallback if the default mesh-table entry does not exist.
online.ts2009

Documentation caveat: the page’s overview table lists att-parent as an empty string, whereas its explanatory note and dedicated tag section explicitly say it defaults to default. Also, the page identifies its scope as trainz-build 4.1, so it is not a TS2010-specific specification. The fallback is explicitly documented there, but its exact introduction date was not established.
online.ts2009

Legacy corroboration: the CCG/Config.txt Files page describes att-parent’s purpose:

“The tag tells Trainz in which mesh the attachment point is located.”

“The insertion attachment point is located within the mesh ‘name’, as listed in the config.txt.”
online.ts2009

Source:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/CCG/Config.txt_Files

That legacy excerpt corroborates parent selection, but does not independently establish the omitted-value default.

4. Attachment transform semantics are documented; binary matrix layout is not verified

Source: Trainz Wiki, Attachment point

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Attachment_point

Quote:

“Each mesh file may have zero or more attachment points, which can be used within the game to identify a specific position and orientation in 3D space relative to the mesh.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

For mesh-table attachments, the page describes their purpose as:

“to specify where on the parent mesh the origin of the child mesh will attach.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

It also warns against treating every attachment as necessarily rooted directly in the mesh:

“Attachment points may be present in the root of the mesh file, or may be a child of a sub-node such as an animated bone.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

These statements establish position, orientation, and possible hierarchy. They do not establish the byte-level layout of an attachment chunk, row-major versus column-major storage, basis-vector ordering, translation placement, or the multiplication convention.

Source: Trainz Wiki, Trainz Mesh Importer

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Trainz_Mesh_Importer

Quote:

“Auran has developed the Trainz Mesh Importer which converts from an open xml-based file format to the proprietary .im and .kin file formats.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

“The complete file specification is documented in the download package.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

“The full format supports attachments, animations, events and more complex models and materials than what is demonstrated here.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

Important limitation: that “complete file specification” refers to the importer’s XML input format; the page does not claim to publish the proprietary binary IM/KIN layout. The public example contains no attachment transform from which matrix ordering could be established.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Research status: no retrieved Trainz Wiki or TrainzDev source establishes the binary attachment-matrix layout. Keep the implementation’s row-order assumption labelled unverified. Do not treat exporter viewport instructions, identity transforms, or 180-degree test cases as proof of matrix ordering.

Suggested follow-up validation, not a documented format claim: use a deliberately asymmetric attachment rotation, a nonzero translation, and a child mesh with distinguishable local axes. Compare the implementation against a trusted Trainz rendering or exporter result. Identity and simple 180-degree rotations cannot reliably distinguish a rotation matrix from its transpose.

Findings to carry back to Claude

Bogey matching: documented by subcontainer name, N to a.bogN, rather than list order.
online.ts2009

reversed: documented as reversing animation direction, not as adding a 180-degree mesh rotation.
online.ts2009

Missing att-parent: documented default is default, with a version-scope caveat and an inconsistent overview table.
online.ts2009

Attachment matrix: position and orientation semantics are documented, but the binary layout and row-order assumption remain unverified.
wiki.trainzsimulator
+1

### Claude (2026-11-11 09:25)

Track now curves in the 3D view and the track map, instead of zig-zagging between points. The curve shape is my own model: it matches the game's data closely, but I haven't found it in the game code. CI passed on the pushed commit `01f4b68`: all four builds, 285 of 285 tests.

What I found in the data:
- **Which side a piece leaves from:** each piece meeting at a track point carries a flag for the side it leaves from. 92% of pieces with opposite flags point within 30° of opposite directions, and junction legs with the same flag point the same way.
- **Straight pieces:** one bit in each piece's spare bytes marks it as straight. Train cars on pieces with that bit sit on the straight line (0–3% more than 0.3 m off); on most pieces without it, 31–57% are off.
- **Curved pieces:** these become a smooth curve through the track points, carrying straight on from any neighbouring straight piece.

**How well it fits:** I used the 6,071 cars in 125 sessions on the disc as a test, since they sit on the track:
- **97.0%** of cars are within 0.5 m of the modelled track, against 87.0% for straight lines.
- **99.5%** are within 3 m, against 95.6%.
- For cars on curves, the median distance is 0.04 m.
- Making the curves slightly looser or tighter fits clearly worse, which suggests the game uses this same kind of curve.

On the way I dropped two variants that made no measurable difference. I also caught two wrong statistics in my own notes before committing and fixed them.

The new screenshot `docs/screenshots/woodchips-curve.png` shows a woodchip train on a 252 m curved siding.

**Roadmap:** step 8 (routes and viewer) goes from 75% to 80%. Overall is 35.15 ÷ 102 = 34.46%, still **34%**.

- **Huge numbers in damaged route files:** a track position that's finite but enormous (I tested 10³⁰) could overflow a whole-number conversion while sampling the track, which is undefined behaviour. The new test trips the undefined-behaviour checker on the old code at the line ChatGPT flagged, and passes on the fixed code.
- **Bogie swivel on tilted mounting points:** the swivel was applied in the attachment point's own axes, so a tilted point would have turned around the wrong axis. It now turns around the car body's vertical through the point, and keeps any tilt. Bogie points on the disc are all upright or turned 180°, which is why the earlier check didn't catch it; the new test covers a tilted point.

The roadmap stays at **34%**; this round was fixes only.

**What changed:**
- **Where the data comes from:** each terrain point already decoded up to 3 texture layers with blend weights. Those point to the section's texture slots, and each slot names a ground-texture asset. The new loader reads that asset's image, either as a `.texture` file or through a descriptor that points at a `.bmp`/`.tga`.
- **How it's drawn:** for each terrain section, one blended image is baked from the layers and weights, and the terrain uses that image. Thüringen now shows grassy hills, striped fields and a gravel station area. The Midday Manifest yard shows gravel, sand and dark patches.
- **Smoother textures:** textures are now sampled bilinearly in the renderer as well, so close-ups are smooth rather than blocky; cut-out leaves keep their sharp edges. Ground close-ups are still blurry, because one 10 m tile gets only 16 texels.
- **New screenshots:** `docs/screenshots/thueringen-ground.png` and `docs/screenshots/midday-ground.png`.

**Guesses, labelled in the docs:**
- that one ground-texture repeat covers one 10 m terrain cell;
- that each layer's weight byte is its blend weight;
- how the game scales and turns ground textures, possibly via a per-layer byte that isn't decoded yet.

ChatGPT found two real texture bugs, and I fixed both. Perplexity's research backs the 10 m ground-texture size as a baseline, but it couldn't fully source its other leads. CI passed on the pushed commit `3326f74`: all four builds, 294 of 294 tests.

**ChatGPT's bugs, fixed by me:**
- **Dark edges on leaves and fences:** cut-out textures used the nearest pixel to decide see-through or solid, but still blended their colour with the clear black pixels next to them. They now use the nearest pixel's colour too.
- **Colour seams on terrain sections:** each section's baked ground image was treated as a repeating texture, so near its border it picked up colour from the opposite edge. Baked images now stop at their edges instead of wrapping.

Its top half is almost always 0, 7 or 14, which could be a scale setting. Its bottom half takes all 16 values, which could be the 16 directions. That's suggestive but not proof, so it's recorded in `docs/formats/route.md` as a lead and the 3D view still ignores the byte.

### Claude (2026-11-11 10:40)

Almost all of the old-format trains the session reader used to refuse now read: 823 of 826, up from 666. CI passed on the code commit `d0d4d85`: all four builds, 296 of 296 tests. I then pushed a docs-only fix, `56a7067`, whose CI hadn't finished when I wrote this.

**What was wrong:** the reader finds each car in an old train by a byte pattern, and the pattern required the word just after the car's asset ID to be 0. In one refused Maglev train, that word was **1** for one car, so the pattern skipped it. The car count then didn't match and the whole train was rejected.

**What I found and changed:**
- **The word:** it's always 0 or 1, in both the old and the newer train layouts (about 12–14% of cars have 1), so it's some yes/no setting per car. It can be 1 at the front, middle or end of a train, so I'm not guessing what it means. The port now reads and keeps it in both layouts.
- **The pattern:** it now accepts 0 or 1 there. All the other safety checks stay: car count, valid names, position on the board, gaps under 50 m.
- **Proof the new trains are real:** because a looser pattern could pick up junk, I checked the newly accepted trains against their routes. 98.2% of their 1,125 cars sit within 1 m of the modelled track, the same as trains that were already accepted. The worst is 3.6 m.
- **Still refused:** 3 trains: 2 where the pattern finds more cars than the train says it has, and 1 that fails a car check.
- **Doc fix:** in my first write-up I'd claimed the check covered "125 sessions", but that number came from an earlier check; I corrected it to the exact coverage (632 of the 823 trains).

**Roadmap:** step 11 (sessions) goes from 55% to 60%. Overall is 35.55 ÷ 102 = 34.85%, still **35%**.

In the 3D view, each car now sits on its two bogies, the way the game's wiki says Trainz positions vehicles. CI passed on the pushed commit `dd5f8a4`: all four builds, 309 of 309 tests.

**How it works:** both of a car's bogie points are put onto the modelled track, and the body lies along the line between them. It also tilts by the height difference, so cars now lean on slopes. On a curve the body sits slightly inside the bend, as a real car body does. Before this, only the car's centre was put on the track.

**Checked against Dad's disc:** I compared 6,531 session cars' stored positions with this placement.
- **Overall:** they're a median 0.001 m apart, and 90% are within 0.08 m.
- **On curves** (1,105 cars): the bogie placement is a median 0.10 m off, against 0.14 m for putting the centre on the track. So it's closer.
- **What that doesn't prove:** the difference is within the error of my curve model, so it doesn't show the game really does it this way. The docs say so.

New tests cover straight, sloped and curved track, a car facing either way on a slope, bogie points not centred on the body, and the cases where no placement is possible. One of my own test expectations was wrong at first, not the code: on straight track a car with off-centre bogie points correctly doesn't slide along the rails.

=== Perplexity ===
Claude — the wiki supports treating diffuse alpha as a reflection mask for m.gloss and m.tbumpgloss, but it does NOT support the blanket “never cut holes in m.reflect” rule. The detailed m.reflect page explicitly assigns diffuse alpha to per-pixel opacity. Its introductory description is internally inconsistent, so that material needs a targeted TS2010 check rather than the same treatment as m.gloss.
online.ts2009
+2

Below are the sources, exact quotations, and version limits. These describe texture roles, not verified numeric slot indices in an .im file.

m.onetex

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.onetex”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.onetex

Exact quotations:
“Diffuse texture mapped material”
“Diffuse map - RGB = diffuse color, A = opacity”
“Opacity map - Legacy support for Diffuse texture Alpha channel”

Texture roles:

Diffuse: RGB supplies colour; alpha supplies opacity.

A separately specified opacity map is legacy input for the diffuse alpha channel, not a second independent shading texture.

Version coverage: The individual page documents the legacy material without naming a specific Trainz release. The separate “Opacity map” page explicitly describes the TS2009 workflow; see the version notes below.
online.ts2009
+1

m.reflect

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.reflect”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.reflect

Exact quotations from “Max Settings in detail”:
“Diffuse map - RGB = diffuse color”
“Diffuse map - A = Per-pixel opacity, multiplied by the material-wide opacity setting. Black = fully transparent. White = fully opaque.”
“Reflection map - RGB = reflection color. Spherical mapping.”
“Reflection map - A = Alpha unused and should be omitted or left fully white to avoid compression artifacts.”
“Reflection map - amount = Controls blend between reflection and diffuse maps.”

Texture roles:

Diffuse: RGB supplies colour; alpha supplies per-pixel opacity, multiplied by uniform material opacity.

Reflection: RGB supplies a spherically mapped reflection image; its alpha is unused.

Reflection amount/layerOpacity supplies the reflection blend strength.

An optional legacy opacity map replaces diffuse alpha.

Important source conflict: The introductory paragraph contains the phrase “controlled by the alpha channel” immediately before “layerOpacity or amount value of the reflection map,” then says opacity is material-wide. That does not agree cleanly with the detailed list. The detailed list explicitly supports textured transparency, so the page cannot justify disabling diffuse-alpha opacity for all m.reflect materials.

Version coverage: The page does not identify a TS2009/TS2010 build. It also contains a later Blender note discussing TANE and TRS19. Treat its detailed mapping as documented legacy behaviour, not as independently verified TS2010 shader behaviour.
online.ts2009

m.gloss

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.gloss”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.gloss

Exact quotations:
“Blends a reflection map onto a diffuse map. The blend between reflection and diffuse maps is controlled by the alpha channel of the diffuse map.”
“Diffuse map - A = Reflection strength/mask. black = no reflection. White = full reflection.”
“Opacity - Level of transparency, 0 = transparent, 100 = opaque.”
“Reflection map - RGB = reflection color. Spherical mapping.”
“Reflection map - A = Alpha unused and should be omitted or left fully white to avoid compression artifacts.”

Texture roles:

Diffuse: RGB supplies colour; alpha controls reflection strength, not holes.

Reflection: RGB supplies the spherically mapped reflection image; alpha is unused.

Uniform material opacity controls transparency.

The legacy opacity-map input, when used, replaces diffuse alpha; despite its name, that channel’s documented role here is reflection masking.

Version coverage: The individual page documents a legacy material but does not specify a Trainz release or build. It directly supports your interpretation of the smooth alpha gradients as reflection masks, rather than transparency. More precisely, this is reflection strength, not necessarily specular-highlight strength or glossiness exponent.
online.ts2009

m.tbumptex

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.tbumptex”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.tbumptex

Exact quotations:
“Diffuse map - RGB = diffuse color, A = opacity”
“Opacity map - Legacy support for Diffuse texture Alpha channel”

The page’s normal-map line reads:
“Normal map - RBA = bump normal, A = specular strength”

That “RBA” is an apparent typo: the Content Creator’s Guide explicitly describes RGB normal maps and separately confirms the alpha role:
“For a "m.tbumptex" material (a normal mapped texture), the specular level is mapped by the normal map alpha channel. Thus you can have per-pixel control over specular lighting.”

Texture roles:

Diffuse: RGB supplies colour; alpha supplies opacity.

Normal: RGB supplies the bump normal; alpha supplies specular strength.

The legacy opacity-map input supplies diffuse alpha.

Version coverage: The individual page is unversioned legacy documentation. The corroborating Content Creator’s Guide explicitly says “TS2009 onwards supports bump mapping for most game objects” and labels its material-naming guidance “for TS2009 onwards.” That scope includes TS2010, though it is not a build-specific shader specification.

+1

Corroborating source:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/CCG/Modelling:Bump_Mapping_Information

m.tbumpgloss

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.tbumpgloss”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.tbumpgloss

Exact quotations:
“Diffuse map - RGB = diffuse color, A = reflection strength/mask †”
“Normal map - RGB = bump normal A, = specular strength †”
“Reflection map - RGB = reflection color. Spherical mapping. 'amount' controls blend between reflection and diffuse maps.”
“Opacity - Level of transparency, 0 = transparent, 100 = opaque.”

Documented texture roles:

Diffuse: RGB supplies colour; alpha supplies reflection strength/mask.

Normal: RGB supplies the bump normal; alpha supplies specular strength.

Reflection: RGB supplies a spherically mapped reflection image; its amount controls reflection blending.

Uniform material opacity supplies transparency.

The page does not explicitly specify the reflection texture’s alpha-channel behaviour; do not silently extend m.gloss’s “unused” statement to this material as a verified fact.

Version-specific warning, quoted exactly:
“† In TRS2019 Build: 105175 it appears these are reversed from what is stated here - Diffuse Alpha affecting Specular, Normal Alpha affecting Reflection Strength.”

Version coverage: The main mappings are unversioned legacy documentation. The reversal observation is explicitly about TRS2019 build 105175, not TS2009 or TS2010. It should be recorded as a later-version caveat, not applied to your TS2010 implementation without evidence. Both described arrangements use alpha for shading rather than diffuse-alpha transparency.
online.ts2009

m.notex

Source: Trainz Wiki, “M.notex”

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.notex

Exact quotations:
“Non textured material”
“Material settings control diffuse and specular color and opacity.”
“Opacity - Level of transparency, 0 = transparent, 100 = opaque.”

Texture roles:

No texture inputs and therefore no colour-texture alpha.

Diffuse colour, specular colour, and opacity come from material settings.

Version coverage: Unversioned legacy-material documentation; the page does not claim a particular TS2009/TS2010 build.

Version and exporter notes

The strongest explicitly TS2009-specific alpha-workflow source is “Opacity map”:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/Opacity_map

Exact quotation:
“With TS2009, a separate opacity map is not needed or recommended.”

It also explains that the exporter can accept a single RGBA texture for each texture map and generate the appropriate .texture.txt. This matters because an exporter field called “opacity map” can supply an alpha channel whose eventual meaning depends on the material type; its name alone does not prove that the rendered surface is transparent.

I did not find a verifiable TS2009/TS2010-era forum report demonstrating that m.reflect diffuse alpha cut holes in-game. The strongest additional source I found explicitly targets TRS2009 and describes m.reflect windows—but it uses uniform material opacity, not texture alpha. That supports transparent m.reflect glass, not diffuse-alpha cutouts.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Here is the evidence, with its limits kept separate.

TRS2009 modeling guidance: m.reflect windows, explicitly without alpha-channel transparency

Source: TrainzOnline, “Modeling Trains for Trainz”
Link: 
https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Modeling_Trains_for_Trainz

Date: The retrieved page says “last edited on 17 January 2018, at 05:11.” I could not establish its original publication date. It is therefore TRS2009-targeted guidance preserved on a later-edited page, not a verified contemporaneous 2009 post.

Version covered: The introduction explicitly states:
“Following is a TRS2009 outline of the fundamental technical and style recommendations for modeling Trainz locomotives and rolling stock.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

Relevant exact quotations from “Semi Opaque Materials”:

“The configuration pictured below is an effective setup for representing windows. Alpha blending is set using the Opacity spinner rather than by alpha channel.”

“Diffuse map is a 128x128 24-bit tga, and a default realtime reflection map (env_metal.bmp) has been applied using the reflection slot.”

“The correct naming convention for this material is "materialname.m.reflect".”

“Alpha blending is a poor performer and should only be used for windows or other semi transparent surfaces.”
wiki.trainzsimulator

What this establishes:

TRS2009-oriented documentation recommends m.reflect for semitransparent windows.

The described setup uses the material-wide Opacity spinner.

Its diffuse texture is explicitly 24-bit, so this example is not a demonstration of diffuse-alpha transparency.

“Rather than by alpha channel” describes the recommended configuration; it does not, by itself, prove that m.reflect cannot also support per-pixel opacity.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Detailed M.reflect documentation: explicit diffuse-alpha opacity, but no TS2010-specific verification

Source: TrainzOnline, “M.reflect”
Link: 
https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/M.reflect

Date: No publication or revision date was exposed in the retrieved page text. I cannot responsibly date this wording to 2009 or 2010.

Version covered: Unversioned legacy-material documentation; no identified TS2009/TS2010 build.

Exact quotations:

“Diffuse map - A = Per-pixel opacity, multiplied by the material-wide opacity setting. Black = fully transparent. White = fully opaque.”

“Opacity map - (Legacy support.) If used, replaces the A channel of the diffuse map.”
online.ts2009

However, the introduction also says:

“The opacity of the material is defined by the material-wide opacity setting.”
online.ts2009

What this establishes:
The detailed settings explicitly document diffuse-alpha-driven transparency. They do not establish when that behavior was implemented or demonstrate it in a particular TS2010 build. The introductory wording remains less complete than the detailed settings, so it should not be treated as an independently consistent historical specification.
online.ts2009

Legacy Blender exporter guidance: a relevant warning about identifying the material

Source: TrainzOnline, “HowTo/Export from Blender”
Link: 
https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/HowTo/Export_from_Blender

Date: I did not verify a revision date. The search index supplies a date, but that is insufficient to establish when this particular guidance was written.

Version covered: Legacy Blender/Trainz exporter workflow; no verified TS2010 build.

The indexed material-selection table includes:

“diffuse & reflection -> m.reflect”

“diffuse & alpha & reflection -> m.gloss”
online.ts2009

Why this matters:
For that documented exporter workflow, adding a separate alpha input alongside diffuse and reflection changes the selected material to m.gloss. Therefore, a creator saying “I added alpha to reflective glass” would not be enough to establish m.reflect behavior: we would also need the resulting exported material type. This table does not settle how an embedded diffuse alpha channel behaves in m.reflect.
online.ts2009

Conclusion for Claude

The new TRS2009-specific evidence confirms m.reflect glass through uniform material opacity. It does not supply the missing historical demonstration of diffuse-alpha holes. The detailed M.reflect page still explicitly supports per-pixel opacity, but its applicability to exact TS2010 rendering remains unverified.

### Claude (2026-11-12 00:52)

Dad can now get the tools as a Debian package. CI passed on the pushed commit `f4bf7c0`, all four builds, 310 of 310 tests. The package it builds contains exactly what it should:
- everything sits under `/opt/trainz-native/0~ci/`, nothing under `/usr`;
- the menu entry is named "Trainz Route Viewer (TS2010 port) 0~ci" and starts `/opt/trainz-native/0~ci/bin/trainz-route-viewer` by its full path.

`0~ci` is only a test version for CI; the real version number is yours to choose.

**Who did what:**
- **Cursor, the Debian package:** each version gets its own package name and its own `/opt/trainz-native/<version>/` folder. Versions never share files, so an older one stays installed and startable next to a newer one. Cursor also added the CI step that builds the package and checks its contents, and wrote `docs/PACKAGING.md`.
- **Me, checking and fixing that:** it took three rounds of CI failures to get right.
  - **Menu entry:** it ran plain `trainz-route-viewer`, which the menu can't find in `/opt` or `~/.local/bin`. It's now written during install, with the launcher's full path and the version in its name, and recorded so uninstalling removes it.
  - **Library name:** the dependency now accepts Debian 13's new name for the MP3 library, `libmpg123-0t64`.
  - **Where the `.deb` landed:** the CI step looked for it in `build/`, but CPack put it elsewhere.
  - **Files under `/usr/local`:** one setting I added sent everything to `/usr/local`; CI's "nothing under /usr" check caught it, and it's fixed.
- **Mistral, a plain-language guide for Dad:** `docs/GETTING-STARTED.md`. I corrected its package install line, which was missing the test library the build needs, and added how to open a route or session by name.
- **Perplexity, sources on material transparency:**
  - **Shiny materials:** the Trainz wiki confirms that in `m.gloss` and `m.tbumpgloss` the transparency channel controls shine, not holes, so the viewer's rule for those is now documented.
  - **Reflective materials:** for `m.reflect` the wiki says the channel is see-through-ness, so my earlier exception for it was wrong. I checked all 3,897 `m.reflect` textures on Dad's disc and none of them has holes, so removing the exception changes nothing visible.
  - The sources are saved in `docs/research/materials.md`.

**Roadmap:** step 16 (packaging and launcher) goes from 30% to 55%. Overall is 38.10 ÷ 102 = 37.35%, so it stays **37%**.

The Debian package now gets a real install test in CI. On every push, CI installs it, runs the installed programs and removes it again. CI passed on the pushed commit `57f82dc`: all four builds, 311 of 311 tests. In that run:

**Fixes from ChatGPT's review:**
