=== Perplexity ===
Claude — research only; no project files changed and no packaging work duplicated.

Recommended starting point: keep resistance coefficients per vehicle, distinguish wheel power from engine power, and cap traction/braking by adhesion on the axles actually involved. Below are usable numbers with their provenance and limitations.

Davis resistance: equation and units

For the implementation, use:

R = A + Bu + Cu*u

where:

u = absolute speed in m/s.

R = resistance magnitude in N.

A has units N.

B has units N·s/m.

C has units N·s²/m².

Apply the resulting force opposite motion. These are straight, level-track resistance coefficients; grade and curve resistance are separate. Do not mix total-force coefficients with coefficients quoted in lb/US ton or N/tonne. Szanto explicitly distinguishes “per unit resistance from total R, in units of force.”
rosap.ntl.bts

Freight resistance: an engineering-paper baseline

Source: Frank Szanto, Downer Rail, “Rolling Resistance Revisited,” Conference on Railway Excellence, 2016, sections 2–3, equation 4.

https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/79083/dot_79083_DS1.pdf

Quote:
“R = 6.5m + 80n + 0.046vm + 0.096 v² (N)”

Here m is vehicle mass in metric tonnes, n is axle count, and v is km/h. The speed convention is confirmed by the paper’s worked table. This is the paper’s metric rendering of AAR RP-548, not the separate AREA 1970 formula sometimes also called “Modified Davis.”
rosap.ntl.bts

Converted for the game’s m/s convention:

A = 6.5m + 80n
B = 0.1656*m
C = 1.24416

Example: one loaded 80-tonne, four-axle freight wagon:

A = 840 N.

B = 13.248 N·s/m.

C = 1.24416 N·s²/m².

For ten identical wagons, the wagon portion of the train is:

Mass = 800 tonnes.

A = 8,400 N.

B = 132.48 N·s/m.

C = 12.4416 N·s²/m².

Add locomotive resistance separately.

These are algebraic conversions and an illustrative consist, not measurements of a particular ten-wagon train. They reproduce the source’s roughly 2,154 N per wagon at 100 km/h.
rosap.ntl.bts

Important qualification: this is a defensible baseline, not a universal truth. Szanto’s operational-data fits give lower resistance for some Australian heavy-haul stock. Table 5 gives mass-dependent constants of 4.0–4.5 N/tonne versus RP-548’s 6.5, and concludes that the linear-speed term may be negligible. Quote: these are not the “‘right’ values to use for all cases.” Keep coefficients configurable rather than hardcoding one “freight” constant.
rosap.ntl.bts

Passenger resistance: a usable historical preset, with weaker provenance

I found an explicit passenger-car coefficient set, but its accessible reproduction is simulator documentation rather than an independently inspected original textbook or test paper. Treat this preset as provisional historical coaching stock, not a validated modern passenger train.

Source: Coals to Newcastle, “Train Resistance,” original Davis formula and vehicle-type table.

https://www.coalstonewcastle.com.au/physics/resistance/

Quoted table entry:
“Passenger Car (Vestibule ends) | 120 | 0.03 | 0.00034”

The columns are frontal area in ft², linear-speed coefficient, and aerodynamic factor. Substituting into the reproduced Davis expression gives:

r = (1.3 + 29/w) + 0.03V + [0.00034a/(wn)]V²

where:

r = lbf per US short ton.

V = mph.

w = US short tons per axle.

n = axles.

a = frontal area in ft².

One US short ton = 2,000 lb, not a metric tonne.
coalstonewcastle

Illustrative 50-US-short-ton coach, four axles, 120 ft²:

Mass ≈ 45.36 metric tonnes.

A ≈ 805.1 N.

B ≈ 14.93 N·s/m.

C ≈ 0.9081 N·s²/m².

For six such coaches, excluding the locomotive:

Mass ≈ 272.16 tonnes.

A ≈ 4,830.6 N.

B ≈ 89.55 N·s/m.

C ≈ 5.4487 N·s²/m².

These are converted illustrative values, not measured six-coach-train coefficients. The documentation cautions that the original Davis model describes older journal-bearing stock and reports satisfactory results over 5–40 mph. Do not present this as a modern high-speed-train calibration.
coalstonewcastle

For a stronger modern modelling reference, Alturbeh et al.’s LABRADOR paper, section 3.4, supplies passenger-train resistance estimation equations including power/trailer mass and aerodynamic geometry. However, its printed power unit in the B expression differs from another published reproduction, so I would not silently turn that expression into a numeric default without resolving the unit discrepancy.
wikipedia
+1

Locomotive starting tractive effort and power

Source: Siemens Mobility, Vectron X AC/DC/MS manufacturer specifications.

https://www.mobility.siemens.com/global/en/portfolio/rolling-stock/locomotives/vectron/ac-dc-ms.html

Quoted specification rows:
“Starting tractive effort (kN)” — “300 / 320 / 350”
“Max. power at wheel (kW)” — “6,400 (AC)”
mobility.siemens

A reasonable manufacturer-based modern mainline-electric game preset is:

Starting force limit = 300,000 N.

Maximum wheel power = 6,400,000 W.

These are an electric-locomotive example, not a claim that all locomotives have these ratings. Crucially, Siemens specifies power at the wheel: do not deduct a diesel-generator/drivetrain efficiency from this number again.
mobility.siemens

Suggested simplified force envelope:

At rest, use the starting-force and adhesion limits; do not divide by zero.

While moving, cap force by the minimum of starting-force limit, wheel power / absolute speed, and available adhesion.

This is a simplified game envelope, not the manufacturer’s complete traction curve.

Braking deceleration: well-sourced passenger settings

Source: Hamid Alturbeh, Julian Stow, Gareth Tucker and Alan Lawton, “Modelling and Simulation of Train Brake System in Low Adhesion Conditions,” Institute of Railway Research / Rail Delivery Group, section 3.5.

https://pure.hud.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/14343760/Modelling_and_Simulation_of_Train_Brake_System_in_Low_Adhesion_Conditions.pdf

Quote:
“notch 1, 2, 3 and Emergency, corresponding to values of train brake demand of 3%, 6%, 9% and 12% of g”
pure.hud

Using the paper’s g = 9.81 m/s²:

Notch 1: 0.2943 m/s².

Notch 2: 0.5886 m/s².

Full service / notch 3: 0.8829 m/s².

Emergency: 1.1772 m/s².

These are brake demands, not guaranteed achieved decelerations. Adhesion, gradient, resistance and brake response affect the result. The paper models pneumatic delays and wheel-slide protection and compares its passenger-unit simulations with historic Class 153/158 brake tests; it also states that low-adhesion validation was limited.
pure.hud

Recommendation: use these four values for the initial passenger brake controller. A rounded 0.6 m/s² ordinary-service setting corresponds closely to notch 2, rather than treating full service as the normal driving setting.
pure.hud

Freight limitation: I did not establish an equally strong, directly verified universal freight-service deceleration in this pass. Do not label 0.5 m/s² a sourced freight standard. Freight braking needs its own consist/brake-system calibration and application delay, rather than simply inheriting the passenger settings.

Adhesion limits

Use an effective adhesion coefficient mu, dimensionless:

Maximum wheel–rail longitudinal force = mu * normal load.

For traction, include only driven axles. For braking, include only axles receiving the relevant brake effort; locomotive dynamic braking does not gain adhesion from unpowered wagon axles. The LABRADOR model’s wheelset-level force and brake allocation provides the appropriate modelling structure.
pure.hud

Ordinary dry/wet examples:

Source: Min-Soo Kim, Korea Railroad Research Institute, “Study on the Adhesion Characteristic between Wheel and Rail using the Scaled Test-bench,” International Journal of Mechanics, volume 9, 2015, pp. 198–205.

https://www.naun.org/main/NAUN/mechanics/2015/a462003-149.pdf

Quote:
“0.25~0.30 in dry and 0.18~0.2 in wet.”

These ranges are reported comparisons with an actual experiment, not identical to the paper’s own bias-corrected scaled-rig measurements. That distinction matters; use them as indicative ranges rather than guaranteed available adhesion.
naun

More severe contamination:

Source: “Iron Oxide and Water Paste Rheology and Its Effect on Low Adhesion,” Tribology Letters, 2021.

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11249-021-01549-0

Quote:
“a very low traction coefficient minimum of 0.02”

That result concerns a particular hematite/water paste in laboratory testing. It supports a severe contamination scenario, not the assertion that ordinary rain always produces mu = 0.02.
link.springer

Suggested configurable game presets:

Dry: mu = 0.25.

Ordinary wet: mu = 0.18.

Severe oxide/water contamination: mu = 0.02.

The first two select values within the reported ordinary-condition ranges; the third is a deliberately severe laboratory-supported scenario. These are modelling choices, not universal railway constants.
link.springer
+1

Implementation cautions for G2

Store every coefficient with its equation convention. “C = 0.096” is wrong if copied from the freight source directly into an m/s equation; it becomes 1.24416 after converting the squared speed term.
rosap.ntl.bts

Sum total forces, or compatible total-force coefficients, across vehicles. Do not sum N/tonne coefficients and then multiply by total train mass; Szanto explicitly warns against that treatment of aerodynamic resistance.
rosap.ntl.bts

Keep grade separate, and eventually evaluate it along the consist rather than only at the locomotive. LABRADOR evaluates vehicle gradient at each vehicle’s geometric centre.
pure.hud

Keep rolling resistance separate from wheel–rail adhesion: the former resists motion; the latter limits usable traction and braking.
rosap.ntl.bts
+1

A brake can hold only within its capacity and available adhesion. If the downhill force exceeds those limits, rollback is physically possible; “brakes never push backwards” must not become “brakes can hold any slope.”
pure.hud

Bottom line for Claude: the freight RP-548-derived preset, Siemens electric-locomotive ratings, passenger brake notches and configurable adhesion presets are ready to use with the caveats above. The historical passenger resistance preset is usable for an explicitly old-style coach, but modern passenger resistance and freight braking remain calibration gaps—not verified universal defaults.

Claude — I found a usable named-train resistance preset, resolved the LABRADOR power-unit mismatch, and found a freight braking case with an explicit consist, brake percentage, application lag, propagation speed and filling time. The freight case is emergency braking in P position, not ordinary service braking; that distinction must remain in the implementation.

+2

Passenger resistance: named Shinkansen coefficients from Rochard & Schmid

Source:
B. P. Rochard and F. Schmid, “A review of methods to measure and calculate train resistances,” Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part F: Journal of Rail and Rapid Transit, 214 (2000), pp. 185–199.
DOI: 10.1243/0954409001531306

Readable reproduction of the original paper:

https://www.scribd.com/document/848584104/TrainResistanceRochard-Schmid

These are equations in the original journal paper, not a simulator-site transcription. The provenance has one qualification: Rochard & Schmid report Japanese railway test-derived equations supplied by T. Maeda through personal communication; they do not publish the underlying raw measurements.
scribd

Equation convention:

R = A + Bv + Cv²

R is total train resistance, not resistance per tonne. For the following coefficients, R is in N and v is in m/s. The paper itself prints these particular Shinkansen equations with R in kN; I have multiplied all three coefficients by 1,000.
scribd

A. Shinkansen Series 100, complete 400 m, 886 t train, ballasted track

Source location: section 3.3, p. 191, equation 24.

Printed equation:
R_kN = 11.06 + 0.2232v + 0.0156168v²

Implementation coefficients:
A = 11,060 N
B = 223.2 N*s/m
C = 15.6168 N*s²/m².
scribd

B. Same Series 100 train, slab track

Source location: equation 23.

Printed equation:
R_kN = 11.06 + 0.10944v + 0.0156168v²

Implementation coefficients:
A = 11,060 N
B = 109.44 N*s/m
C = 15.6168 N*s²/m².
scribd

The track distinction changes B in the reported equations. Do not silently combine the slab-track B with a claim that the preset represents the ballasted-track case.
scribd

C. Shinkansen Series 200, complete 300 m, 712 t train

Source location: equation 25.

Printed equation:
R_kN = 8.202 + 0.10656v + 0.0119232v²

Implementation coefficients:
A = 8,202 N
B = 106.56 N*s/m
C = 11.9232 N*s²/m².
scribd

Note the exact C: 0.0119232 in the paper’s kN convention, not 0.0119322 as appears in some teaching-material reproductions.
scribd
+1

Measurement provenance:
The paper states that resistance is estimated by a “run-down test” and coefficients are determined by the “least-squares method.” It then attributes these specific Japanese equations to T. Maeda.
scribd

Recommendation:
Use the Series 100 ballasted-track equation as a specifically named high-speed EMU preset, not a universal passenger-coach default. These are historical high-speed multiple units, rather than present-generation commuter stock. This closes the “only old coach numbers from a simulator site” gap, but does not establish resistance for an arbitrary modern four-car regional unit.
scribd

There is also an internal source inconsistency worth retaining in metadata: equation 23’s accompanying text says 886 t, whereas Table 1 later lists 856 t for its Series 100 comparison. The coefficients above reproduce equations 23–25 directly; I would not derive per-tonne coefficients from that conflicting mass information.
scribd

LABRADOR B term: the printed MW label is inconsistent with its source

LABRADOR original paper:
Hamid Alturbeh, Julian Stow, Gareth Tucker and Alan Lawton, “Modelling and Simulation of Train Brake System in Low Adhesion Conditions.”

https://pure.hud.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/14343760/Modelling_and_Simulation_of_Train_Brake_System_in_Low_Adhesion_Conditions.pdf

On p. 12, equation 22 prints:

B = 0.18TM + NT + 0.005NP*PW

It then defines PW as “PW [MW] is the train power.” B is labelled N*s/m.
pure.hud.ac

However, Rochard & Schmid’s section 2.2 explicitly says that power in these Armstrong–Swift equations is expressed in “kW,” and equation 3b uses the same numerical coefficient, 0.005. Their stated convention is masses in tonnes, power in kW and B in N*s/m.
scribd

Therefore, the source-consistent implementation is:

B_Ns_per_m = 0.18*trainMass_t
+ trailerCarCount
+ 0.005powerCarCounttotalTrainPower_kW

Equivalently, if the stored power is MW:

B_Ns_per_m = 0.18*trainMass_t
+ trailerCarCount
+ 5.0powerCarCounttotalTrainPower_MW

The correction is to use kW with 0.005, or MW with 5.0. Using MW with 0.005 makes the power-dependent contribution 1,000 times too small. This is a correction of LABRADOR’s published equation/definition mismatch; it does not prove what units its unpublished executable model actually used.
scribd
+1

Also retain the applicability restriction: Rochard & Schmid conclude that Armstrong–Swift is suitable for British-size trains with a power-car-to-trailer ratio of 1:3 or less, but “not suitable for trains with a predominance of powered axles.” For the named Shinkansen presets above, use the reported train-specific coefficients instead of regenerating them with Armstrong–Swift.
scribd

Freight braking: a fully specified European air-braked case

Source:
N. Bosso, M. Magelli and N. Zampieri, “A numerical method for the simulation of freight train emergency braking operations based on the UIC braked weight percentage,” Railway Engineering Science 31 (2023), pp. 162–171.
DOI: 10.1007/s40534-022-00296-9

Open institutional copy:

https://iris.polito.it/retrieve/handle/11583/2974770/969379

This is an original modelling paper calibrated against UIC 544-1 stopping distances and compared with an earlier fluid-dynamics model. It is not a report of newly measured stopping tests. The authors explicitly say, “the model is validated in emergency braking operations”; service braking requires separate tuning.
iris.polito

A concrete loaded-freight benchmark

Table 1, simulation 5:

Leading locomotive: E402B, 89 t.

Wagons: 20 Shimmns wagons, each 80 t.

Total physical train mass: 1,689 t.

Wagon length: 12.64 m each; locomotive length: 19.42 m.

All vehicles braked in P position.

Initial speed: 100 km/h.

Train braked-weight percentage: 74.0%.

UIC 544-1 reference stopping distance as reported by the authors: 739.3 m.

Their LTDPoliTo simulated stopping distance: 705.3 m.

Earlier Pugi fluid-dynamics-model stopping distance: 635 m.
iris.polito

The E402B itself has braked weight 79 t, versus physical mass 89 t. Do not confuse that locomotive-specific ratio with the 74.0% whole-train figure. The Shimmns empty/loaded changeover means wagon brake percentage varies with loading.
iris.polito

Application dynamics

Table 3 supplies the following calibrated values for the paper’s P-position emergency-braking cases:

t_app = 1 s
Meaning: lag from brake command until cylinder pressure starts rising.

v_air = 200 m/s
Meaning: propagation speed of the pressure-drop wave along the train.

t_fill = 5 s
Meaning: brake-cylinder filling time used in the model.
iris.polito

These are separate quantities, not one interchangeable “application delay.”

The paper’s equations 5–7 give a convenient implementation structure:

localDelay = t_app + distanceBehindLeadingLocomotive / v_air

tau = t_fill / ln(20)

For elapsed time u = t - localDelay:

If u < 0, brake-block pressing force is zero.

Otherwise, brake-block pressing force is:
F_block(t) = F_block_max * (1 - exp(-u/tau))

With this definition, t_fill is the time after local onset at which the exponential reaches 95% of its asymptotic pressing force. Actual wheel braking force is then calculated from brake-block pressing force and the shoe friction coefficient; the cast-iron shoe coefficient depends on speed and block load.
iris.polito

Important: 200 m/s is the calibrated propagation parameter of this model, not a universal service-brake propagation speed. Likewise, 5 s belongs to these P-position cases, not slow G-position freight braking.
iris.polito

What deceleration can legitimately be attached to that freight case?

For the 20 × 80 t Shimmns case, the UIC-reference stopping distance implies a distance-equivalent constant deceleration:

a_equiv = v_initial² / (2*stoppingDistance)
= (100/3.6)² / (2*739.3)
≈ 0.522 m/s².

Using the paper’s simulated 705.3 m instead gives approximately 0.547 m/s². These are my derived whole-stop equivalents from its published distances, not quoted instantaneous or fully developed brake decelerations. They incorporate the effect of brake development and the stopping trajectory.
iris.polito

Consequently:

It is defensible to say: “This specified 1,689 t European freight consist has a UIC-reference emergency stopping-distance equivalent of about 0.52 m/s² from 100 km/h, in P position.”

It is not defensible to say: “UIC specifies 0.5 m/s² as normal freight service braking.”

Do not use 0.522 m/s² as a fully developed brake plateau and then add the published delays on top while expecting the same stopping distance; that would count the delay effect twice.
iris.polito

Slow G-position freight: separately supported filling-time range

A railway test-rig research paper explicitly reports that UIC 540 requires brake-cylinder filling times “between 18 and 30 s for freight trains in G regime.”
ingegneriaferroviaria

Source:
“Calibrazione e messa a punto di un banco a rulli multiasse,” Ingegneria Ferroviaria, July–August 2020, pp. 501–523:

https://www.ingegneriaferroviaria.it/web/sites/default/files/IF_7-8_20_SeT_pag501_523.pdf

This supports the 18–30 s G-regime filling-time range through a research paper citing UIC 540; I have not directly verified the underlying UIC clause in a readable original copy

=== Perplexity ===
Public-source research handoff for Claude — 11 November 2026

I researched only the public-source part. No project files or original game data were read, changed, run or patched. This does not independently verify the reported implementation, tests or roadmap percentage.

Main finding: public documentation is strongest for content configuration, enginespec parameters, soundscripts and the TrainzScript API. It is substantially weaker for the exact binary layouts needed by a replacement engine. Community source code supplies useful evidence for textures and mesh/animation serialization, but I did not establish a complete public TS2010 specification or reader for every requested format.

Dates below distinguish a source’s explicit historical scope from its publication date. All links were consulted on 11 November 2026. Where an original publication or revision date could not be verified, I say so rather than treating search-engine dates as authoritative.

Version boundaries and source quality

The official Content Creator’s Guide landing page explicitly says its data model and technology were valid up to TRS2009-SP1. This makes the CCG a relevant historical baseline, not proof of every TS2010 detail. The same page directs authors toward the newer KIND and container specifications. Conversely, pages hosted at online.ts2009.com can contain much later additions; the hostname alone does not establish TS2009 compatibility.
online.ts2009

Source:
https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/Content_Creator's_Guide

Date/version: historical documentation through TRS2009-SP1; current wiki revision date not independently established.

For the project, distinguish:

Documented authoring semantics.

A community implementation of particular binary structures.

Behaviour actually checked against this TS2010 install.

Only the last category establishes compatibility with Dad’s particular data.

.ja archives

Status: archive identity supported; complete public binary specification not established in this research.

A Trainz forum thread dated 22 November 2006 explicitly discusses “Jet Archive” files containing TRS2004 world content. It is useful historical evidence for the archive family, but not a TS2009/TS2010 byte-layout specification.
auran

Source:

https://forums.auran.com/threads/how-to-modify-the-jet-archive-files.866/

Date/version: 22 November 2006; TRS2004.

The historical TRS2004 content-creation guide also discusses extraction from Auran .JA files, while warning that this was unsupported. That establishes historical use, not a documented decoding contract.
scribd

Source:

https://www.scribd.com/document/160116848/Trainz-2004-DRAFT-Content-Creation-Procedures

Date/version: document identifies itself as TRS2004-era material; original publication date not verified.

What remains unestablished publicly here:

TS2010 archive header and directory-entry structures.

Compression or encryption rules, if any, for particular archive variants.

Filename encoding, alignment and integrity fields.

A verified open-source TS2010 .ja reader.

Do not substitute TZarc documentation for .ja documentation. SilverGreen93’s TZarchiver explicitly handles .tzarc, and its README notes that Trainz 2022 introduced compressed TZarc v2, which it does not support. That is a different archive target, not evidence that TS2010 .ja files use that layout.
github

https://github.com/SilverGreen93/TZarchiver

Date/version: repository publication date not verified; explicitly discusses Trainz 2022 and TZarc versions.

.im and .pm meshes

Status: roles documented; useful community binary-writing implementation exists; complete TS2010 binary coverage unproven.

The historical Content Creator’s Guide identifies .im as Indexed Mesh and .pm as the older Progressive Mesh format. It says progressive meshes remain usable in Trainz Classics but recommends .im for new content. This is historical compatibility evidence, not a binary field specification.
archive

Source:

https://archive.org/stream/manualzilla-id-5634944/5634944_djvu.txt

Date/version: Trainz Classics-era guide; original publication date not verified.

The official Trainz Mesh Importer documentation is especially important: it describes .im and .kin as proprietary binary formats and provides an open XML interchange format converted by Auran’s importer. The XML describes authoring inputs; it must not be presented as the on-disk .im/.kin specification. The current page also marks this importer obsolete as of trainz-build 4.5.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Source:

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Trainz_Mesh_Importer

Date/version: historical pre-build-4.5 workflow, with a later obsolescence notice; original publication date not verified.

Community source:

https://github.com/rileyzzz/BlenderIMExporter

This exporter writes .im directly, rather than delegating to TrainzMeshImporter.exe. Its README lists vertex/index data, UVs, normals, optional tangents and bounds, material data, and separate .kin animation generation. It also explicitly warns about wide-string representations that other tools sometimes mishandle. This is a valuable implementation reference and an immediate source of parser edge cases. It is a writer, however—not an established general-purpose .im reader.
github

Date/version: repository publication date not verified; modern Blender 2.8+ tool targeting legacy Trainz/JET formats, with some later-engine features. TS2010 compatibility must be checked feature by feature.

Community tools:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/Trainz_Tools_by_PEV

http://trainz.shaneturner.co.uk/tutorials/index.php/home/utilities/pevsoft-trainz-tools/pm2im

PEV’s PM2IM converts .pm to .im, and Trainz Mesh Viewer renders textured meshes and complete traincars. Shane Turner’s PM2IM page identifies version 2.06 as released on 29 March 2015. These are evidence of working community decoders/converters, but the consulted pages do not establish that their implementation source is available.
online.ts2009
+1

Remaining gaps: a complete .pm layout, exhaustive .im chunk/version coverage, and assurance that unusual materials, skinning and string encodings match all TS2010 assets.

.kin animation

Status: official authoring pathway documented; community serializer available; complete binary specification not established.

The official importer converts XML animation descriptions into proprietary .kin files. BlenderIMExporter independently generates .kin files for armature or dummy-object hierarchies. Together these give useful references for animation structure and serialization, but do not establish complete TS2010 decoding coverage.
wiki.trainzsimulator
+1

Sources:

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Trainz_Mesh_Importer

https://github.com/rileyzzz/BlenderIMExporter

Date/version: same scopes as section 3.

Remaining gaps: exhaustive animation record types, interpolation semantics and all binary version variants. Treat anything beyond inspected source and tested assets as unverified.

.texture and .texture.txt

Status: authoring descriptor documented; compiled texture reader source available.

The official Texture file page distinguishes the human-editable ASCII .texture.txt descriptor from the resource name used in configuration: references omit the final .txt. It documents source-image options and internal texture formats, including DXT compression. The current page also includes newer capabilities, so its entire feature list must not be assumed valid for TS2010.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Source:

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/Texture_file

Date/version: current, cross-version documentation; original publication date not verified.

Important distinction: a resource called “name.texture” in config does not by itself prove that a physical compiled name.texture file is present. The documented authoring resource may be represented by name.texture.txt plus source image data.
wiki.trainzsimulator

Open-source reader:

https://github.com/rileyzzz/TrainzTexture

The repository describes itself as a work-in-progress texture import/export library, contains a test project, and identifies its code as GPL-3.0. Its license text identifies Trainz texture parsing work copyrighted in 2021. This is a concrete reader candidate, but I did not audit its implementation or establish which TS2010 texture variants its tests cover.
github

Date/version: 2021 copyright; exact supported Trainz releases not established.

Community tool:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/Trainz_Tools_by_PEV

Images2TGA reads Trainz images, handles DXT-compressed textures, and supersedes Texture Viewer 2 and Texture2TGA. The page mentions subsequent support for two T:ANE texture versions, reinforcing the need to distinguish format generations. It is a practical comparison tool, not a published byte-level specification.
online.ts2009

mapfile.gnd, mapfile.obs and mapfile.trk

Status: file responsibilities officially documented; exact binary layouts not established.

The official CCG map example identifies:

mapfile.gnd: ground/topology data.

mapfile.obs: placed-object data.

mapfile.trk: track-layout data.

It also names Trainzmap as a third-party viewer for the track file. That establishes a historical reader existed, not that its source or a complete format specification is available.
online.ts2009

wikibooks

https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Trainz/file_types_by_extensions

Date/version: cross-version community reference; original publication date not verified.

Remaining gaps:

Per-version terrain records and texture-layer encoding.

Object record layouts and identifiers.

Changes between legacy routes, TS2009 and TS2010.

I did not establish an open-source reader covering all three TS2010 map formats. In particular, these public sources do not validate the project’s inferred track-curve model.

profile.dat

Status: session role officially documented; binary layout not documented by the sources found.

The CCG says a Profile is a Session, and that config.txt and profile.dat are generated by Surveyor. Its example explicitly calls profile.dat the session-information file and says it is not human-readable. The example also shows the session’s map-kuid reference.
wiki.trainzsimulator
+1

https://wiki.trainzsimulator.com/wiki/CCG/Example:Profile

auran

https://forums.auran.com/threads/reading-profile-dat-files.40512/

Remaining gaps: binary schema, nested session state, train-placement encoding, rule state, script state and the distinction between initial session data and saved running-game state. I did not verify a public open-source TS2010 profile.dat reader.

enginespec and traincar physics keys

The CCG TrainCar reference documents mass and references such as enginespec and enginesound. Its rolling-stock example has engine 0 and still references an enginespec asset: enginespec is not limited to powered locomotives.

TS2009-specific runtime documentation:
“New TrainzScript Features — TS2009” explicitly identifies changes from trainz-build 2.9, including cross-asset script inclusion and separate global and active-module VMs. Global scripts persist until exit; the active-module VM owns route/session/gameplay context. A compatible implementation therefore needs more than source parsing or decryption.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Stack:** C++20, CMake, GoogleTest, ASan/UBSan plus `float-cast-overflow`, CI with gcc/clang × release/asan-ubsan on Debian 13, plus a clean `debian:13` package-runtime job.
   - **Local builds without cmake:** objects in `/tmp/tzb` for tools, `/tmp/tzt` for sanitizer tests. gtest is at `/var/tmp/gtestdeb/root/usr`. SDL headers are at `/var/tmp/sdldeb/root/usr/include/{SDL2,x86_64-linux-gnu}`; link against `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libSDL2-2.0.so.0`.
   - **CI warning flags:** `-std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wnon-virtual-dtor -Wold-style-cast -Wcast-align -Woverloaded-virtual -Werror`.
   - **Data:** `/var/tmp/trs_install` (Base.ja, Data.ja, Builtin) and `/var/tmp/trs_builtin/app/Builtin/*.ja`; `XDG_DATA_HOME=/var/tmp/shots/...` for renders; PNG compression with `python3 -I /var/tmp/obsscripts/shrink.py IN OUT 1`.
   - **Renderer (`SceneRender`):**
     - textures with a mip per triangle, perspective-correct and bilinear sampling;
     - nearest texel for cut-outs (`alphaTest`), `clampEdges` for baked terrain;
     - `sampleTextureBilinear` is public and NaN-safe;
     - texture sides limited to 8192.
   - **AssetMeshes:**
     - textures (≤128 px, plus file mips); cut-out heuristic `wantsAlphaTest` (≥5% clear, ≥1% solid, <50% in between);
     - `materialMayCutOut` returns false only for m.gloss and m.tbumpgloss (documented); m.reflect alpha is opacity;
     - `ATCH` attachment points, `LocalFrame` (Direct3D row order assumed), attached parts (`att`, with `att-parent` defaulting to `default`);
     - bogies (`bogey` / `bogeys` N ↔ `a.bog<N>`; `reversed` only reverses the animation, so no turn is added);
     - `.pm` fallback; reskin textures by file name (`reskinFiles`);
     - SpeedTree billboards (SRT 05.0.1 header box at byte 36 × mesh-scale mean, the atlas's first cell, speck skipping, `kAtlasSide=512`).
   - **Track:**
     - link flag = vertex side; stretch `rest[0]` bit 0x20 = straight (observed);
     - Hermite curve model (tangent scale 1, carries straight on from straight neighbours): 97.0% of session vehicles within 0.5 m;
     - `TrackLocator` (bounded coordinates, `kMaxCoordinate=30e6`);
     - `placeOnBogies` (tilted midpoint in all three coordinates); `headingAlong`; `swivelAboutModelZ`.
   - **GroundTextures:** per-section bake from vertex layers and weights; 10 m tile assumed (forum source).
   - **Sessions:** old-train pattern accepts `wordAfterKuid` of 0 or 1 → 823 of 826 trains read.
   - **Route viewer, launcher, packaging:**
     - `route-viewer` (SDL, software renderer) with `--list` / `--route` / `--session` by name, exit codes 3 and 4, `--frames`, `--png`, mouse and gamepad (`GamepadSlot`, tested with virtual controllers), and `--drive`;
     - launcher `trainz-route-viewer` (symlink-safe `mktemp` setting write, refuses a data folder inside the game folder);
     - CPack DEB under `/opt/trainz-native/<version>/`, collision-free package names (`cmake/TrainzPackageName.cmake`), `CPACK_SET_DESTDIR` + `CPACK_INSTALL_PREFIX`, a `.desktop` file written at install time with the full Exec path and the version in its Name.
   - **Sim (`src/sim`):**
     - `TrackNetwork`: arc-length positions, `advance` across vertices, junction `switches`, `locate`;
     - `stepTrain`: traction limited by force, power and adhesion; brakes capped by adhesion; Davis resistance; grade given as the sine;
     - `makeTrain` from `VehicleSpec`; sourced presets (RP-548 freight wagon, Vectron, Shinkansen Series 100, passenger brake notches).
   - **Game (`src/game`):**

=== Perplexity ===
Public-source research only; no files read or changed. The sources establish the junction/trackside behavior and signal configuration model, but not the TS2010 .obs/.trk binary layout. In particular, API direction constants and asset configuration values must not be treated as proven on-disc encodings.

Source scope and era

TS2010-era material:

The legacy Content Creator’s Guide pages document mojunction and mosignal. The mojunction page was last modified June 5, 2011, and its example targets trainz-build 2.7. This is useful contemporary documentation, not a verified copy of a separately published TS2010 CCG.
online.ts2009

The CCG kinds index explicitly describes junction control levers as attached to track junctions, and signals as assets defining supported aspects, light points, coronas and track offsets.
online.ts2009

Sources requiring version caution:

KIND MOSignal was last edited in 2018 and explicitly mixes older configuration examples with TANE-onward guidance.
online.ts2009

Current Class Trackside and Class JunctionBase documentation describes useful runtime relationships, but does not establish when every method or signature became available. JunctionBase explicitly labels ownership features as introduced for Interlocking Towers. Do not backport those features into TS2010 based on this page alone.
online.ts2009
+1

The modern “How to Control Junctions/Signals in Sessions” tutorials explicitly target TANE, TRS19, TRS22 and Trainz Plus, not TS2010.
online.ts2009
+1

How mojunction ties to track

The legacy CCG describes mojunction as the asset kind for junction control levers. The CCG kinds index says these levers attach to track junctions and can replace the default lever. Its trackside value supplies a lateral offset in metres: negative places the lever left of track centre, positive right. That offset is not a branch-selection value.
online.ts2009
+1

Links:

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/CCG/Kind:MOJunction

https://online.ts2009.com/mediaWiki/index.php/CCG/Kinds

The current runtime API distinguishes two cases:

A spline-track junction has a junction lever object.

An embedded junction in fixed track has an embedded node; its MapObject is the fixed-track parent.
JunctionBase.GetGameObject() and GetMapObject() document these distinctions. GetDebugString() can expose an associated MapObject node ID, but that is not evidence of a particular .trk vertex-ID field or serialized linkage.

Junction direction: selection versus storage

Surveyor’s Junction Direction tool changes the default direction used in Driver by clicking the junction arrows. Green denotes the default direction. Adding a third track produces a three-way turnout with three direction arrows. This documents user-visible default selection, not its binary representation.

The current JunctionBase API defines:

DIRECTION_LEFT = 0

DIRECTION_FORWARD = 1, described as straight on for three-way points

DIRECTION_RIGHT = 2

DIRECTION_BACKWARD = -1, the leading approach

DIRECTION_NONE = 3, no direction/error

GetDirection() returns the current direction; ToggleJunction() advances to the next valid direction. These are runtime API constants, not verified TS2010 route-file enum values.

The page explicitly warns these codes are not always the same as Trainz junction-direction constants. These are Junction Kit conventions, not universal mojunction semantics.

The legacy CCG defines MOSignal as a train signal whose configuration specifies supported aspects, the light points used for each aspect, and corona details. It also permits a track offset.

The later KIND MOSignal page supplies this concrete configuration structure:

kind mosignal

type Trackside

function TrackSignal

signals { ... }: numbered supported states and their display settings

lights { ... }: numbered light definitions with corona resources

Per-state entries including light, speed, flash and flash-offset

Behavior keys including distant, home, repeater, always-controlled, double-blocking, overlap and overlap-track-circuited

Its example declares trainz-build 2.8, but the page itself is later and is not proof that every listed key behaves identically in TS2010.

Important distinctions for implementation:

The container is “signals”, plural. The numeric state name selects an aspect; its “light” value selects a light definition. State numbers and light indices are different namespaces. The example maps state 1 to light 2, state 4 to light 1, and state 8 to light 0.
online.ts2009

The documented default logic distinguishes state 0, absolute stop, from state 1, permissive stop. Including state 1 rather than 0 allows the autopilot to pass permissively and queue behind the train ahead. State 4 is used for a fixed distant/caution indication. Thus reducing all red displays to the same operational state loses behavior. These details come from the later documentation and need TS2010 validation.
online.ts2009

“light -1” declares a valid state without illuminating a light. Assets without declared states have a deprecated pre-v1.3 fallback using a.red, a.orange and a.green attachments. A parser should distinguish “no visible light” from “unsupported state.”
online.ts2009

“trackside” is the lateral offset in metres, not a protected-track ID. Negative means left, positive right.

How a signal identifies the track it guards

KIND MOSignal says signals are placed on a track and participate in the signalling system. Current Class Trackside documentation makes the runtime association explicit:

GetTrack() returns the track segment on which the object is located.

BeginTrackSearch(direction) searches along the track using the trackside object’s orientation relative to its attached track.

This supports a track-attachment-plus-orientation model, rather than “choose the nearest rail to the visible signal mesh.” The lateral offset alone does not encode that attachment or facing direction. The exact TS2010 serialized attachment, position-along-track and orientation fields remain unverified.

The later signal documentation also explains that custom signal scripts can override DetermineUpdatedState() and ApplyUpdatedState(). Signals are updated in response to dependencies discovered through GSTrackSearch, rather than simply on a fixed periodic timer. That matters for eventual compatibility with scripted assets, but it is later-source guidance, not a decoded TS2010 algorithm.

How AI and player trains follow junction settings

For ordinary user selection, the Surveyor help explicitly connects the green/default junction direction with subsequent driving in Driver.

For AI routing, the legacy Junction Kit documentation says AI can negotiate its multi-node fixed-track junctions and switch the junctions without script interference. It also makes a useful distinction: the kit’s junction links operate on manual switching and are ignored by AI. Consequently, “linked switch movement” and “AI-selected route” are not necessarily the same mechanism. These claims are specifically about the kit, not all assets.

### Summary of What Was Covered:
1. **Existing Foundation from `.obs` and `.trk`:**
   - **Object Class Registrations**: Factory bindings for `jnOb` (`bOnj` / `mojunction`, 10,138 objects on disc) and `sgOb` (`bOgs` / `mosignal`, 13,806 objects on disc), along with related trackside classes (`tsO2`, `tsOb`, `spOb`, `mkOb`, `tgOb`).
   - **Placement & Coordinates**: Standard `PlacedObject` base block (8-byte header `0x03` + `0xff000000`, board index, local $x, y, z$ in metres). Highlights that 79–88% of junctions and 75–82% of signals sit within 1 m of the terrain or nearest vertex.
   - **Yaw = 0.0 Convention**: Confirms that signals and junctions store $yaw = 0.0$ in the object record and infer orientation from their associated track piece.
   - **Embedded Names**: Notes that junction payloads contain plain-text names (e.g., `"Single Track"`, `"Airport Junction 2"`).
2. **Track Topology & Curvature:**
   - **Vertex Slots (`tkVx`)**: 4-link records, identifying that vertices with 3 links (12,242 across the disc) closely match `jnOb` counts. References the **38 junction-like vertices** identified on the test route among 794 pieces.
   - **Turnout Legs & Side Flags**: Link flags denote vertex departure side; 83% of same-flag pairs point within 30° of each other, forming the diverging legs of turnouts.
   - **Simulation State**: Explains `sim::TrackNetwork`'s current behavior (defaults to straightest continuation; switchable via `net.switches[vertex] = piece`).
3. **Session Rules:**
   - Mentions session `profile.dat` `BHVR` rules (`"Set Junctions"` configuring initial switch states via embedded `.chump` settings) and session trackside deltas in `profile.obs`.
4. **Known / Guess / Left Reference Table:**
   - Categorizes each aspect of junctions and signals into **Known** (registration, base layout, vertex topology, simulation branching), **Guess** (track-relative orientation), and **Left** (`jnOb` vertex tie mechanism, switch direction state, lever meshes/animations, `sgOb` track attachment, aspect rules/signals, and AI path reservations).

  - `trackside` is a sideways offset in metres, not a link to a track;
  - a signal's states and its lights are separate lists;
  - the direction numbers in the scripting docs aren't the values stored in route files.

- **Later:** a faster graphics-card renderer, sounds, cab views and scripts.

```cpp
std::optional<JunctionSetting> junctionSetting(const TrackVertex& v) {
    if (v.links.size() < 3) return std::nullopt;
    JunctionSetting j;
    for (std::size_t k = 0; k < v.links.size(); ++k) {
        std::size_t same = 0;
        for (const auto& l : v.links) same += l.flag == v.links[k].flag ? 1 : 0;
        if (same == 1) {
            if (j.trunk >= 0) return std::nullopt;            // two lone flags
            j.trunk = v.links[k].item;
        } else if (same + 1 != v.links.size()) {
            return std::nullopt;                              // e.g. a crossing: two pairs
        } else {
            j.legs.push_back(v.links[k].item);                // legs in slot order
        }
    }
    if (j.trunk < 0 || j.legs.size() < 2 || v.lastByte >= j.legs.size()) return std::nullopt;
    j.selected = v.lastByte;
    return j;
}
// TrackNetwork constructor, per vertex:
if (const auto j = junctionSetting(v); j && pieces_.count(j->legs[j->selected]) != 0)
    switches[index] = j->legs[j->selected];
// toggle: the next way after the current setting, wrapping to the first
std::int32_t TrackNetwork::toggle(const JunctionAhead& j) {
    if (j.ways.empty()) return -1;
    const auto sw = switches.find(j.vertex);
    auto at = sw == switches.end() ? j.ways.end() : std::find(j.ways.begin(), j.ways.end(), sw->second);
    const std::int32_t next = at == j.ways.end() || at + 1 == j.ways.end() ? j.ways.front() : *(at + 1);
    switches[j.vertex] = next;
    return next;
}
```

@ChatGPT here's the core of the signal code from `e3f0f6d` (`src/sim/Signals.cpp`) for review. Check:
- the block boundaries;
- signals for the other direction being skipped;
- the strict "more than 1 cm ahead" rule, so a signal doesn't find itself;

Report findings with line numbers.
```cpp
std::optional<SignalSystem::Ahead> SignalSystem::firstAhead(const TrackPosition& start, double maxDistance) const {
    std::optional<Ahead> found;
    net_.walk(start, maxDistance, [&](const TrackNetwork::Span& s) {
        const auto [b, e] = byPiece_.equal_range(s.piece);
        for (auto it = b; it != e; ++it) {
            const TrackPosition& at = signals_[it->second].at;
            if ((at.direction >= 0 ? 1 : -1) != s.direction) continue;   // other direction
            const double along = (at.offset - s.from) * s.direction;      // metres past the span's entry
            const double span = std::fabs(s.to - s.from);
            if (along < 0 || along > span) continue;
            const double d = s.startDistance + along;
            if (d > 0.01 && (!found || d < found->distance)) found = Ahead{it->second, d};
        }
        return !found;  // the first span holding one has the nearest
    });
    return found;
}

void SignalSystem::update(const std::vector<Occupied>& occupied) {
    std::multimap<std::int32_t, double> taken;
    for (const auto& o : occupied) taken.emplace(o.piece, o.offset);
    std::vector<std::optional<std::size_t>> next(signals_.size());
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < signals_.size(); ++i) {
        const auto ahead = firstAhead(signals_[i].at, kMaxBlock);
        const double blockEnd = ahead ? ahead->distance : kMaxBlock;
        bool busy = false;
        net_.walk(signals_[i].at, blockEnd, [&](const TrackNetwork::Span& s) {
            const auto [b, e] = taken.equal_range(s.piece);
            const double lo = std::min(s.from, s.to), hi = std::max(s.from, s.to);
            for (auto it = b; it != e && !busy; ++it) busy = it->second >= lo && it->second <= hi;
            return !busy;
        });
        aspects_[i] = busy ? Aspect::Stop : Aspect::Clear;
        next[i] = ahead ? std::optional<std::size_t>(ahead->index) : std::nullopt;
    }
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < signals_.size(); ++i)   // second pass: Stop is final after pass 1
        if (aspects_[i] == Aspect::Clear && next[i] && aspects_[*next[i]] == Aspect::Stop) aspects_[i] = Aspect::Caution;
}
```
The driving readout calls `update` twice a second. The occupied points are the player's train (`game::trainOccupies`: lead, then every 5 m back over its length) plus the session's other trains (`game::standingTrains`). @ChatGPT here are the parts of `eba8de3` that your excerpt left out, for review. Please check that the yaw maths puts the lamps on the side facing oncoming trains, and that `stateForAspect` can only return a state that's in the list. Report findings with line numbers.
```cpp
// src/content/SignalAsset.cpp
std::optional<int> stateForAspect(const SignalLook& look, int aspect) {
    if (look.states.empty()) return std::nullopt;
    auto inRange = [&](int lo, int hi) -> std::optional<int> {
        const auto it = look.states.lower_bound(lo);
        return it != look.states.end() && it->first <= hi ? std::optional<int>(it->first) : std::nullopt;
    };
    const auto stop = inRange(0, 3), caution = inRange(4, 7);
    const auto clear = look.states.count(8) != 0 ? std::optional<int>(8) : inRange(9, 9999);
    if (aspect <= 0) return stop ? stop : look.states.begin()->first;
    if (aspect == 1) return caution ? caution : stop ? stop : look.states.begin()->first;
    return clear ? clear : caution ? caution : stop ? stop : look.states.rbegin()->first;
}
// src/game/RouteDrive.cpp: orientSignals: model +y along the signal's direction of travel
o.yaw = static_cast<float>(p->heading - std::numbers::pi / 2);   // p = net.point(attachment, direction)
// signalLamps: a lamp's model point (t[0], t[1], t[2]) placed like addPlacedMesh does
const double c = std::cos(o.yaw), s = std::sin(o.yaw);
out.push_back({o.worldX() + c * t[0] - s * t[1], o.worldY() + s * t[0] + c * t[1], o.z + t[2], rgb});
```
The test is `RouteDrive.SignalsTurnToTheirTrackAndLightTheirLamps`. It puts a signal for travel toward −x, and a lamp at model y = −0.2 should land 0.2 m toward +x, facing trains coming from +x.

@ChatGPT here's the near-plane clipping fix from `6d0e680` (`src/view/SceneRender.cpp`) for review. Please check the cut-point interpolation, and whether any triangle with exactly one vertex in front can come out with the wrong winding. That can't drop pixels here, because the rasteriser accepts both windings. Also check the int clamping. Report findings with line numbers.
```cpp
const double nearCut = Projector::kNear * 1.001;          // kNear = 1 m
for (const auto& t : scene.triangles) {
    double d[3]; int inFront = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) { d[i] = proj.depthOf(t.p[i]);      // dot(p - eye, forward)
        if (!std::isfinite(d[i])) { inFront = -1; break; }
        inFront += d[i] > nearCut ? 1 : 0; }
    if (inFront == 3) { drawTriangle(t); continue; }
    if (inFront <= 0) continue;                           // wholly behind
    Vtx poly[4]; int count = 0;                           // Sutherland-Hodgman, one plane
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) { const int j = (i + 1) % 3;
        const bool inI = d[i] > nearCut, inJ = d[j] > nearCut;
        if (inI) poly[count++] = at(i);
        if (inI != inJ) { const double f = (nearCut - d[i]) / (d[j] - d[i]);
            poly[count++] = lerp(at(i), at(j), f); } }   // position, colour, u, v
    for (int k = 1; k + 1 < count; ++k) drawTriangle({poly[0], poly[k], poly[k + 1]});  // 1 or 2 triangles
}
// in drawTriangle: the old "skip if more than 4x the screen" test is gone (cut triangles near the
// camera are big); loops are bounded by the screen, and bounds are clamped as doubles first:
const int x0 = static_cast<int>(std::clamp(minX, 0.0, wMax)), x1 = static_cast<int>(std::clamp(maxX, 0.0, wMax));
```

@ChatGPT here's the core of the AI driver in `69a3428` (`src/game/RouteDrive.cpp`), for review:
```cpp
// stopAhead: nearest of a signal at stop (nextSignal), a point another train takes (walking the
// track ahead along the current junctions), or the line end (where the walk stops short).
void AiDriver::control(RouteTrain& d, const TrackNetwork& net, const SignalSystem* signals,
                       const std::vector<Occupied>& others) const {
    auto& c = d.drive.controls;
    const double v = std::fabs(d.drive.speed);
    c.reverser = +1; c.dynamicNotch = 0;
    double limit = cruise;                                         // 30 km/h
    if (signals) if (auto sg = signals->nextSignal(d.drive.lead, 1500);
                     sg && signals->aspect(sg->index) == Aspect::Caution) limit = cruise / 2;
    if (const auto stop = stopAhead(d, net, signals, others)) {
        const double room = stop->distance - margin;               // 20 m short
        limit = std::min(limit, room > 0 ? std::sqrt(2 * decel * room) : 0.0);   // decel 0.35 m/s^2
    }
    const int topNotch = int(d.drive.spec.notchCurvesN.size()) - 1;
    if (v > limit + 0.3)      { c.notch = 0; c.throttle = 0; c.brake = std::clamp((v - limit) / 2.0 + 0.3, 0.0, 1.0); }
    else if (v < limit - 0.5) { c.brake = 0; c.notch = topNotch > 0 ? std::max(1, topNotch / 2) : 0; c.throttle = 0.5; }
    else                      { c.notch = 0; c.throttle = 0; c.brake = limit < 0.1 ? 1.0 : 0.0; }
}
```

- whether the `room <= 0` case is safe;
- whether a train's own points can leak into its `others` list. The viewer leaves out entry `t + 1`.

### Claude (2026-11-13 11:54)

You can now couple and uncouple trains. It passed GitHub Actions: all four builds and the clean install of the Debian package (commit `e21e642`). All 342 unit tests and the command-line tests pass on this PC.

**New screenshots** (in `docs/screenshots/`):
- `coupling.png`: Midday Manifest's train 5, with 6 cars, driven 300 m up to train 19. It touches at 5 km/h and the 30 cars couple on, making 36. A message at the bottom of the screen confirms it.
- `uncoupling.png`: after stopping, pressing U three times leaves the three rear cars standing, with 33 left. Those cars are behind the camera, so the message is what shows it.

**How it works:**
- **Coupling:** drive slowly (under 7 km/h) into another train and it joins yours in one line. A train facing the other way gets turned round, so its cars are drawn facing the right way. The locomotive's notches come with it.
- **Collisions:** faster than 7 km/h is a collision, and your train stops dead at the point of contact.
- **Uncoupling:** stopped, U leaves your rear car behind, and you can press it again for more. Cars left behind stand still, and the AI never drives them.
- **Throttle on trains without notches:** each W/S press now moves the throttle 10%.

**Bugs I found and fixed while testing on the real route:**
- At about 18 km/h, a train could jump straight through another one between two checks. Contact is now checked before each move, over the full distance the train is about to travel.
- A train's position is the middle of its first car, but my first version treated that as the front buffer. That put the contact point half a car out. It now uses the real buffer ends.

**Progress: 42%.** The train simulation step is up from 28% to 31%; the overall figure doesn't move.

**Still to do:**
- **Brakes and AI:** the trains' own air brakes, and AI trains following the session's orders.
- **Sounds and cab views.**
- **The faster graphics-card renderer,** which would also remove the short pause when the world is rebuilt around the train.

@ChatGPT here's the coupling core from `e21e642` (`src/game/RouteDrive.cpp`). On your three questions:
- **Detached cars:** they go into the viewer's `otherTrains`. That list feeds both contact detection (`findContact`) and signal occupancy (`takenBy`), so detached cars still block other trains and turn signals to stop. The AI skips them because `parked` is set.
- **Mass, brake and notch totals:** after every change they are rebuilt from the cars by `refreshTrain`, which calls `makeTrain` over every car's own spec.
- **Reversed consists:** cars that join turned round have `flipped` toggled and are added in reversed order. In physics a turned-round locomotive still pulls in the train's direction.

```cpp
void refreshTrain(RouteTrain& t) {           // vehicles, length, spec from cars
    t.vehicles.clear(); t.length = 0; std::vector<VehicleSpec> specs; bool anyCurves = false;
    for (const auto& c : t.cars) { specs.push_back(c.spec);
        anyCurves = anyCurves || !c.spec.tractiveCurveN.empty() || c.spec.tractiveForceN > 0;
        if (c.vehicle) { t.vehicles.push_back(*c.vehicle); t.length += c.vehicle->length + 0.5; } }
    if (!anyCurves && !specs.empty()) { auto m = specs.front().massKg; specs.front() = electricLocomotive(); specs.front().massKg = m; }
    t.drive.spec = makeTrain(specs);
}
// lead = first car's MIDDLE; front end = lead + first/2; rear end = lead - (length - 0.5 - first/2)
void coupleTrains(const TrackNetwork& net, RouteTrain& me, RouteTrain& other, const Contact& c) {
    auto theirs = other.cars; std::vector<RouteTrain::Car> merged;
    if (c.atOurFront) {
        TrackPosition newLead = other.drive.lead;                       // their rear touches: same facing
        if (c.theirFront) { theirs = turnedRound(theirs);               // reverse order, toggle flipped
                            newLead = lastVehicleMiddle(net, other); newLead.direction = -newLead.direction; }
        merged = theirs; merged.insert(merged.end(), me.cars.begin(), me.cars.end()); me.drive.lead = newLead;
    } else {
        if (!c.theirFront) theirs = turnedRound(theirs);                // their rear touches our rear
        merged = me.cars; merged.insert(merged.end(), theirs.begin(), theirs.end());
    }
    me.cars = merged; me.drive.speed *= myMass / (myMass + theirMass); refreshTrain(me); other.cars.clear();
}
std::optional<RouteTrain> uncoupleRear(const TrackNetwork& net, RouteTrain& me, std::size_t n) {
    // the last n cars (at least one stays) -> a parked train, braked, its lead behind our new rear end
}
```

**New screenshot: `docs/screenshots/air-brake.png`.** The train is coming off 64 km/h with the brake applied and then held ("lap"). The readout shows "BRAKE 77% (LAP, PIPE ~49 PSI)" at 59 km/h.

**How it works:**
- **Pressures from your files:** each locomotive's engine file lists its brake pipe pressures: fully charged, the first brake step ("initial"), and full braking ("full service"). Your train uses its locomotive's values.
- **The brake handle** works on TS2010's own keys: A applies, Z holds, Q releases, Pause is emergency.
  - The handle changes the pressure in the brake pipe.
  - The pipe responds more slowly on longer trains.
  - The brakes follow the pipe: none when it's fully charged, full braking at the "full service" pressure.
  - Emergency empties the pipe at once.
- **On Midday Manifest:** the pipe drops from about 70 psi to 49 and then 43 psi, and the brake goes from 14% to 77% to 100%.

**What's my guess, not the game's:**
- **The psi figures:** the files use a unit I couldn't pin down. Converting assumes the usual 90 psi main reservoir, and those numbers are only for the readout.
- **The timing:** full braking in about 7 s and release in about 20 s are my own choice. The files' detailed pipe and reservoir sizes aren't used yet.
- **AI trains** still set their brakes directly rather than through the air brake.

On ChatGPT's point about the brakes: I'll describe it as a **simplified air-brake model using the asset pressure settings**, not a real air brake. Here's the core, from `src/game/Drive.cpp` (commit `a3b86d9`):
```cpp
double AirBrake::step(BrakeHandle::Position h, double seconds, std::size_t cars) {
    const double dt = finite(seconds) && seconds > 0 ? min(seconds, 10.0) : 0.0, span = charged - full;
    switch (h) {
    case Application: equaliser = max(full, min(equaliser, initial) - span / 7.0 * dt); break;  // initial reduction at once
    case Lap: break;
    case Release: equaliser = min(charged, equaliser + span / 20.0 * dt); break;
    case Emergency: equaliser = 0; break;
    }
    const double tau = 1.0 + 0.05 * cars;                        // the pipe lags more on longer trains
    pipe = h == Emergency ? 0.0 : pipe + (equaliser - pipe) * min(1.0, dt / tau);
    return demand();   // clamp((charged - pipe) / (charged - full), 0, 1); 1 when vented
}
```
The tests are `AirBrake.PipeFollowsTheHandleAndTheBrakesFollowThePipe` and `AirBrake.LongerTrainsRespondSlowerAndBadPressuresAreIgnored`.

That run was killed again, and this time it's my bug, not just this PC's 7.6 GB of RAM. In the shunting route-finder, a reversal on a long piece of track made the "distance so far" go *down*. ### Claude (2026-11-14 10:02)

ChatGPT found a real hole and it's now fixed. A train doing a coupling move could slip past a red signal if it was close to the train it was joining, even with an unrelated train standing in between. Now it only does that when nothing else is between it and that train. The change passed GitHub Actions on commit `0e8f0d1` (all four test builds and the clean install of the Debian package), and all 359 unit tests pass on this PC.

ChatGPT's test now checks both cases:
- **Another train in between:** the engine stops at the red signal, short of it.
- **Nothing in between:** the engine passes the signal at walking pace, up to the train it's joining.

The test fails on the old code, so it catches the hole. Nothing changed on screen this round, so the latest pictures (`ai-shunting.png` and the ones before it) are still current.

**Will the graphics get better?** Yes, though mostly through one big step I haven't started yet, not gradually.

Right now everything is drawn by a simple renderer I wrote that runs on the processor (CPU), not the graphics card. That's why it looks basic:
- Textures are shrunk to at most 128 pixels, which is why things look blurry up close.
- Lighting is simple shading only: no shadows, no shine, no night.
- Trees are flat cut-outs, and the sky is a plain gradient.
- It manages only about 5–7 frames a second.

The fix is a **graphics-card renderer** (OpenGL), which would use the R9 390 in your dad's PC. That should give smooth frame rates and full-resolution textures. After that it can add proper lighting and shine, fog and a longer view distance, and later night and weather.

Everything you see (trains, buildings, ground, signals) already comes from your original TS2010 files. So the goal is to look like TS2010 itself, not beyond it. Effects the game does with its own shaders, like water and some shine, would need extra work.

It's the biggest single job left on the driving side. I'd suggest doing it next, after I fix why the coal train stops just short of coupling at the end of its shunt. Tell me if you'd rather have the better graphics first.

**Progress: 44%.**
